entries.text:
Scope

A reported zero resistance means that a specified measurement cannot resolve a resistive voltage under its current, geometry and acquisition conditions. It is evidence within a detection limit, not a measurement of a mathematically exact zero. Keep the measured signal, correction and uncertainty together; a display reading of zero does not specify all three. The uncertainty framework below is separate from a microscopic theory of superconductivity. 

Record transition onset, midpoint and the operational zero criterion separately. A conducting path need not occupy the whole specimen. As a simple counterexample, two ideal parallel channels have R{\mathrm{eff}}=R1R2/(R1+R2): one zero-resistance channel shorts a finite-resistance channel. This circuit result establishes no volume fraction or material identity. Magnetic and thermodynamic probes answer complementary questions.

 Mathematical assumptions

Suppose a corrected voltage estimate is \hat V and the applied current estimate is \hat I. If independently justified intervals satisfy |V-\hat V|\le UV and |I-\hat I|\le UI<|\hat I|, the triangle inequality gives a conditional bound:

\left|\frac{V}{I}\right|\le\frac{|\hat V|+UV}{|\hat I|-UI}.

This is a local interval calculation, not an automatically calibrated confidence statement. If the input intervals have probabilistic coverage, the output statement must retain that coverage model and their dependence. An operational threshold |\hat V|<V{\mathrm{cut}} alone does not establish |V|<V{\mathrm{cut}}. Do not substitute a display digit or a noise standard deviation for a validated bound without explaining the choice. NIST's uncertainty guidance distinguishes uncertainty components, applied corrections and coverage. 

For a fixed linear resistance and equal opposite currents, model the readings as V+=IR+V{0,+}+\epsilon+ and V-=-IR+V{0,-}+\epsilon-. Then

\hat R=\frac{V+-V-}{2I}=R+\frac{V{0,+}-V{0,-}+\epsilon+-\epsilon-}{2I}.

A constant current-even offset cancels. Drift, a current-odd voltage, unequal currents or a changing specimen do not satisfy that cancellation. NIST's shunt report describes a thermoelectric contribution that reverses with the current and therefore survives ordinary reversal averaging. Its apparatus-specific thermal treatment is not a universal correction for superconducting samples. 

With fixed known I, the voltage contribution to standard uncertainty is uR^2=[u+^2+u-^2-2\operatorname{cov}(V+,V-)]/(4I^2). Current uncertainty and model/systematic contributions must be included separately when present. Independent algebra and finite-outcome checks verify this conditional variance and show why assuming uncorrelated errors can fail. The check is not an instrument calibration. 

Converting resistance to resistivity as \rho=RA/L additionally assumes the appropriate homogeneous current path, area A and voltage-contact separation L. Four-terminal geometry does not by itself establish uniform current density. Conversely, a passive lumped loop with constant inductance L{\mathrm{loop}} and resistance obeys I(t)=I0e^{-Rt/L{\mathrm{loop}}}. A measured fractional decay no larger than \varepsilon gives R\le-L{\mathrm{loop}}\ln(1-\varepsilon)/t only under that loop model. Vortex relaxation or changing inductance needs a different treatment.

 Experimental criteria

Halperin and Nelson's 1979 superconducting-film theory describes a vortex-unbinding regime, fluctuation conductivity and nonlinear resistivity. This supports a limited theoretical reference for thin-film analysis, not a universal fit or a pairing-symmetry test. The publisher abstract was checked; its full derivation has not yet been reviewed here. 

Use four-terminal measurements where the time scale and apparatus permit them, and state the actual geometry when they do not. Publish the voltage/current data, detection criterion, field orientation, temperature sweep, bandwidth or integration time and contact configuration. Check current dependence, contact stability and thermal response. Treat these as editorial evidence requirements rather than a claim that one fixed protocol fits every apparatus.

If contacts or backgrounds are subtracted, preserve the original reading and propagate the uncertainty of the subtraction. An independent magnetic or heat-capacity result on a comparable sample helps test a bulk interpretation. A low transport reading alone cannot exclude a connected minority phase, a short or an instrument limitation.

 Limits and disputes

Mitrano and colleagues' earlier author manuscript reports transient optical signatures in driven K3C60 and discusses a high-mobility alternative interpretation. Such spectra do not constitute a direct DC transport measurement. This check covers selected 2015 manuscript passages; the publisher record flags an update whose details have not been verified here. No optical crossover temperature is entered as an equilibrium transition. 

Budden and colleagues complement optics with a 1 ns electrical probe of a driven K3C60 pellet at 100 K. The checked manuscript uses a two-terminal transient measurement with contact resistance calibrated against static four-terminal measurements. Figure 4 explicitly includes a calibration-related systematic uncertainty. A resistance compatible with zero in this driven experiment is not an equilibrium T{c,\mathrm{zero}}. The numerical waveform and complete final journal version were not independently reanalyzed. 

These methods probe different observables and time windows. Keep optical extrapolation to zero frequency separate from electrical response, and distinguish either from long-time equilibrium transport. A very large photoconductivity can motivate further tests without resolving every question about phase coherence or magnetic expulsion.

 Discovery implications

A useful discovery report states which observations would distinguish a superconducting path from a contact artifact, minority phase or alternative conducting state. Repeat under controlled current and magnetic field, retain unsuccessful controls, and seek independent probes of the claimed phase. Field suppression supports an interpretation but does not uniquely identify a pairing interaction.

BCS theory is retained as a microscopic background reference, with its detailed treatment in the linked BCS entry. It is not the source for the measurement bounds or procedural requirements developed here. Keep operational transport evidence, theoretical interpretation and claims of bulk superconductivity distinct.

entries.text:
Scope

Quasiparticle interference (QPI) uses spatial variations in scanning tunneling conductance to constrain electronic states and scattering. Elastic scattering can connect states of equal energy with momentum transfer \mathbf q=\mathbf k'-\mathbf k. A Fourier peak is a feature of a measured response, not a direct photograph of a Fermi surface or a uniquely identified order parameter. Keep the tunneling matrix element, defect channel and preprocessing attached to every interpretation.

In a weak-tunneling description with a sufficiently smooth tip spectrum and matrix element, low-temperature differential conductance can approximate a sample's local density of states. Thermal and instrumental convolution, spatially varying set points and orbital sensitivity can change that relation. A conductance map and an ideal local-density-of-states calculation should not be treated as interchangeable without testing these assumptions.

 Mathematical assumptions

With the convention \tilde g(\mathbf q,E)=\sum{\mathbf r}e^{-i\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf r}g(\mathbf r,E), a translated pattern obeys

g'(\mathbf r,E)=g(\mathbf r-\mathbf r0,E),\qquad\tilde g'=e^{-i\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf r0}\tilde g.

Its Fourier magnitude is unchanged, while its real and imaginary parts generally change. A real map satisfies \tilde g(-\mathbf q)=\tilde g(\mathbf q)^. Independent discrete-transform checks verify both identities, an exactly sampled cosine and sampling aliases. Finite cropping can also change amplitudes; the exact translation identity assumes the whole pattern or periodic data, not two differently cropped fields.

For a periodic lattice with N sites and one defect at the origin, define an ideal electron-block response

\Lambda(\mathbf q,E)=\frac{1}{N}\sum{\mathbf k}[G0(\mathbf k,E)\,T(E)\,G0(\mathbf k-\mathbf q,E)]{11}.

Here G0 is a retarded Nambu Green function and T=[1-Vg0]^{-1}V, with g0=N^{-1}\sum{\mathbf k}G0. The Fourier transform of the spin-resolved electron density-of-states change is

\delta\tilde\rho(\mathbf q,E)=-\frac{\Lambda(\mathbf q,E)-\Lambda(-\mathbf q,E)^}{2\pi i}.

Taking just -\operatorname{Im}\Lambda(\mathbf q)/\pi is insufficient for a general complex Fourier map. It becomes valid with the additional even-in-momentum response condition. Six independent checks compare full real-space resolvent inversion with the scattering expression on a ten-site, fixed-gap model; displaced defects expose the lost phase. This is a normalization and response check, not a cuprate or FeSe simulation. The selected Wang–Lee manuscript supplies the broader scattering framework and explicitly discusses off-shell and matrix-element limits. 

A joint-density-of-states construction counts candidate equal-energy connections but omits scattering amplitudes and coherence factors. In an ideal equal-magnitude, real-gap Fermi-surface limit, scalar and magnetic Born amplitudes contain uu'-vv' and uu'+vv'. Setting u=u'=1/\sqrt2 and v=\operatorname{sgn}(\Delta)/\sqrt2 interchanges their zero/nonzero weights when the relative gap sign changes. This conditional example explains sensitivity to the impurity channel; it does not identify a real defect from one bright peak. 

 Experimental criteria

Hoffman and colleagues' dispersing-QPI manuscript reports Bi2212 conductance imaging at 4.2 K. Selected pages describe two peak families with opposite energy trends and doping-dependent dispersion, interpreted against photoemission information. Its Science DOI ends in 1072640. The inherited DOI ending in 1066974 instead identifies their distinct vortex-core modulation paper; these are not interchangeable evidence.  

Sprau and colleagues' FeSe manuscript reports imaging at 280 mK. The relative-sign analysis uses the real parts at opposite energies, isolates an interband momentum region and places the Fourier origin at a defect. Selected supplementary passages vary the integration area and repeat the analysis on additional impurities. The reported sign inference is conditional on their scattering model and band assignment; it is not an inference from the absolute Fourier intensity alone. 

Report field of view, pixel spacing, spatial drift correction, bias grid, temperature, excitation amplitude, tip condition, set-point protocol and defect selection. Preserve both raw and processed maps. State whether a displayed quantity is a complex transform, its real part, magnitude, power or a ratio: these operations retain different information. Explain normalization, windowing, background removal, symmetrization and peak uncertainties.

 Limits and disputes

For Nx equally spaced pixels of spacing ax, the periodic-transform length is Lx=Nxax and angular-wavevector bin spacing is 2\pi/Lx; the Nyquist bound is \pi/ax. Using cycles per length removes the 2\pi factors. Zero padding interpolates the transform but does not create a larger measured field. A window trades spectral leakage against peak width, so bin spacing alone is not an experimental uncertainty or guaranteed resolving power.

Energy dispersion supports a scattering interpretation only together with band, defect and temperature/field controls. Weak dispersion over a limited window does not by itself prove charge order; Bragg, structural, moire and electronic features can overlap. Conversely, an order and QPI may coexist. The cuprate octet geometry must not be imposed on arbitrary multiband spectra.

The McElroy reference in the pinned chapter used an unrelated biology DOI, nature02269. The correct QPI paper is nature01496; its publisher identity is checked here, while its detailed data remain outside this entry's review. The original source is preserved and the replacement recorded. 

 Discovery implications

Use QPI to compare explicit candidate electronic and scattering models against multiple observables. A useful claim states which alternatives the data discriminate, which are still compatible, and how uncertainty in defect identity or preprocessing changes the result. Combine gap-magnitude constraints with independent bulk and phase-sensitive evidence before assigning a pairing state or mechanism.

entries.title: The Meissner effect and magnetic evidence
entries.summary: Distinguish equilibrium flux expulsion from shielding, then interpret penetration depth and magnetic volume estimates with their geometric assumptions.

entries.text:
Scope

The Meissner effect describes magnetic flux exclusion from superconducting material in the appropriate equilibrium, low-field state. It adds information beyond persistent current or zero resistance. The London brothers explicitly distinguished their magnetic-state condition from an acceleration-only description that can retain the initial field. Their historical equations are used here in a modern SI convention, within a stated local model. 

The 1933 Meissner–Ochsenfeld report compares the external field around tin and lead before and after cooling through the transition. It also describes field retained in the cavity of a hollow lead tube. A field in that cavity is not a measurement of field penetrating the superconducting wall. Selected pages of a reproduction containing the original German and an English translation were checked; the historical experiment was not independently reproduced. 

Separate zero-field-cooled shielding, field-cooled magnetization and hysteresis. A type-II specimen can contain vortices, and pinning can prevent equilibration during cooling or field sweeps. Thus a protocol-dependent signal should not be labeled complete equilibrium flux expulsion. The vortex review supplies qualitative context; it is not a calibration of a particular sample's volume fraction. 

 Mathematical assumptions

In a homogeneous, isotropic, vortex-free local London model, with displacement current neglected, combine the magnetic London relation with Ampere's law and \nabla\cdot\mathbf B=0:

\nabla\times\mathbf j=-\frac{\mathbf B}{\mu0\lambda^2},\qquad \nabla\times\mathbf B=\mu0\mathbf j,\qquad \nabla^2\mathbf B=\frac{\mathbf B}{\lambda^2}.

For a half-space x>0 with parallel surface field B(0)=B0 and bounded field at depth, the solution is B(x)=B0e^{-x/\lambda}. The surface boundary and exclusion of a growing solution matter; the differential equation alone does not specify an arbitrary specimen's field map. These are modern local-model deductions, not a claim that London theory covers every superconducting state. 

For an infinite slab -a<x<a with equal parallel fields on its two faces, no vortices and constant \lambda, the same boundary-value problem gives

\frac{B(x)}{B0}=\frac{\cosh(x/\lambda)}{\cosh(a/\lambda)},\qquad \chi{\parallel}=\frac{\langle B\rangle}{B0}-1=\frac{\lambda}{a}\tanh\!\left(\frac{a}{\lambda}\right)-1.

Here 2a is the full thickness and B0=\mu0Ha. A local finite-difference solution independently checks the field profile and its spatial average. A thick slab tends toward \chi{\parallel}=-1; a very thin slab in this parallel geometry has much weaker shielding even when the entire slab obeys the superconducting model. This is not a formula for a perpendicular-field thin film or a porous specimen.

Demagnetization is a separate shape effect. For an ellipsoid along a principal axis, with uniform scalar susceptibility in SI, let H{\mathrm{int}}=Ha-NM and M=\chi H{\mathrm{int}}. Then

\chi{\mathrm{app}}=\frac{M}{Ha}=\frac{\chi}{1+N\chi}.

For the perfect-diamagnet limit \chi=-1, this gives \chi{\mathrm{app}}=-1/(1-N), for N<1. A sphere has N=1/3, so an uncorrected magnitude of 1.5 is consistent with this ideal geometry, not a 150% superconducting volume. The Prozorov–Kogan manuscript defines the convention and explains why nonellipsoidal specimens need additional treatment. Its numerical arbitrary-shape results are not reproduced here. 

In a single-component carrier convention, \lambda^{-2}=\mu0nsq^2/m^. Count charge, mass and density consistently: pair density is not electron density. For a uniform thin film with thickness d\ll\lambda and negligible dissipative response, the sheet kinetic inductance is Lk=\mu0\lambda^2/d. Equating magnetic-model current response and carrier kinetic energy checks this normalization. Inferring a bulk penetration depth from a sheet response therefore requires thickness and a response model; multiband or nonlocal systems need their corresponding treatment.

 Experimental criteria

Report specimen dimensions, field orientation and amplitude, cooling and sweep history, magnetic moment normalization, background subtraction and the assumed geometry. For AC or microwave probes, include frequency, amplitude and the conversion from the measured response. These are reporting requirements; a successful model inversion is not an independent demonstration of its assumptions.

Hardy and colleagues report a linear contribution to the penetration-depth change of YBa2Cu3O6.95 single crystals over approximately 3–25 K with a 900 MHz resonator. This abstract-scoped observation constrains low-energy excitations. It does not directly measure gap phase or uniquely identify the pairing representation; sample disorder and electrodynamics belong in the interpretation. No transition temperature is extracted here. 

 Limits and disputes

Shielding and expulsion can differ because of field history, geometry, connectivity and pinning. A small signal alone does not distinguish a small superconducting region from a measurement or geometry limitation. Conversely, a connected superconducting shell can screen a nonsuperconducting interior; a shielding measurement alone cannot establish the interior's volume fraction. The historical hollow-tube observation makes the distinction between material and enclosed space especially important. 

Božović and colleagues' overdoped LSCO study is retained as a reference for superfluid-density measurements, but this check confirms its bibliographic identity rather than reanalyzing its scaling data. Do not infer a pairing mediator from a correlation alone. Likewise, a measured total stiffness cannot be decomposed into conventional and geometric contributions merely by changing its label. Follow the dedicated geometric-superfluid-weight entry for that separate model question. 

 Discovery implications

Build a magnetic evidence package around discriminating measurements: cooling history for trapping, dimensions and orientation for demagnetization, thickness for sheet response, and transport or heat capacity on comparable specimens for complementary evidence. Preserve disagreements between probes until sample and analysis differences are tested.

Separate measured magnetic response, the fitted electrodynamic parameters and the microscopic interpretation. This keeps magnetic evidence useful for discovering superconductivity without turning one model-dependent inversion into an unqualified material property or mechanism assignment.

entries.title: Specific heat: the jump, entropy balance and bulk evidence
entries.summary: Read a thermodynamic anomaly with its background, normalization and transition criterion. The BCS jump is a model benchmark, not a universal verdict.
entries.text:
Scope

Heat capacity probes the change of entropy with temperature. A superconducting anomaly can therefore provide a bulk thermodynamic check that complements resistance and magnetic screening. A peak alone does not identify its cause: magnetic, structural and charge-order transitions can also produce anomalies. This article separates an ideal electronic heat-capacity jump from the measured total signal and from an empirical trend across different samples.

Use C on a declared basis: per mole, per unit mass, per volume or for the entire sample. The normalization of the normal-state electronic coefficient \gamman must match. Experiments often measure Cp, while a simple electronic model evaluates heat capacity with a fixed spectrum and volume. Their difference may be small for an appropriate low-temperature solid, but that approximation should be justified when quantitative precision matters.

 Mathematical assumptions

For an isotropic single-band weak-coupling BCS model with a smooth density of states, define the electronic jump on cooling as \Delta Ce=C{es}(Tc^-)-C{en}(Tc^+). Its limiting value is


\frac{\Delta Ce}{\gammanTc}=\frac{12}{7\zeta(3)}\simeq1.426.


Here C{en}=\gammanT in the assumed low-temperature normal state. The number is a model benchmark, not a threshold that every superconductor must pass. Johnston gives the limiting expression in Eq. (22) of the cited author manuscript. 

Entropy follows from dS=C\,dT/T under the specified thermodynamic constraints. For a continuous transition with equal extrapolated zero-temperature entropies in the compared phases,


Ss(Tc)-Sn(Tc)=\int0^{Tc}\frac{Cs(T)-Cn(T)}{T}\,dT=0.


The normal curve below Tc is a defined reference, not a directly accessible zero-field equilibrium phase. Background subtraction and low-temperature extrapolation therefore affect the test. A first-order transition has latent heat and requires a different treatment. Do not force this continuous-transition construction onto such a dataset.

An independent numerical check for this entry solved the constant-density-of-states gap equation, integrated the quasiparticle entropy and differentiated it near Tc. The normalized jump approaches 1.426 as the cutoff and numerical step are controlled; the normalized entropy reaches the normal-state value at the transition. This checks the stated model and conventions, not a material dataset. The entropy and heat-capacity relations are consistent with the selected manuscript equations. 

 Experimental criteria

Start from the measured heat capacity and report addenda, sample mass and calibration uncertainty. A fit such as Cn/T=\gamman+\beta T^2 assumes a linear electronic term and a low-temperature lattice contribution. It can fail if extra excitations or nearby transitions matter. State the temperature interval and uncertainty of the background, and show how another reasonable background changes the inferred anomaly.

A field used to suppress superconductivity is not automatically a perfect normal-state reference. Check whether it reaches the normal state over the relevant range and whether it changes magnetic or other contributions. Use the same units and sample basis in the field and zero-field curves. Show transition width, the chosen thermodynamic Tc and the entropy comparison, rather than only a peak height.

Compare with resistance and screening on the same or demonstrably comparable specimen. A consistent anomaly with the expected field response strengthens the case for bulk superconductivity. Failure to resolve an anomaly may instead reflect sensitivity, sample size, a small superconducting fraction or an incorrect baseline. It leaves thermodynamic confirmation incomplete; it does not by itself establish absence of superconductivity. These are reporting and interpretation criteria from the pinned chapter, not independently verified measurements.

 Limits and disputes

The phenomenological alpha model retains the BCS normalized gap shape while varying \alpha=\Delta(0)/(kBTc) in the thermodynamic calculation. Padamsee and colleagues describe its quasiparticle construction in their abstract. A successful fit is not a microscopic derivation of the interaction. 

Within that model the jump scales as 1.426(\alpha/\alpha{\rm BCS})^2. This does not mean that the entire entropy or heat-capacity curve can simply be multiplied by that factor: the occupation functions also change. Gap anisotropy or multiple coupled bands can alter the normalized jump. Multiple bands do not necessarily broaden a single sharp transition; disorder, phase mixtures and a distribution of local transition temperatures are separate issues. 

Bud'ko, Ni and Canfield report an empirical relation \Delta Cp/Tc\propto Tc^2 for their substituted Ba122 series together with specified literature samples. Equivalently, the jump itself scales as Tc^3 within that comparison. This is a dataset-dependent observation, not a fundamental law or a stand-alone proof of a pairing mechanism. The current check covers the publisher abstract, not a reanalysis of the data. 

 Discovery implications

Use an anomaly to constrain a proposed state together with independent probes. Ask which part of the temperature dependence is reliable, how much of the sample participates, and whether competing backgrounds could produce the same result. Preserve disagreement between probes and the uncertainty in extrapolated quantities.

A useful next experiment resolves a specific ambiguity: a field-dependent background, an uncertain phase fraction, a residual low-temperature term or an alternative gap distribution. Comparing a single normalized jump to 1.426 cannot uniquely select gap symmetry, coupling strength or a mediator. These are model-discrimination questions, not new experimental findings.

entries.text:
Scope

Isotope substitution changes nuclear mass while keeping the element the same. The resulting response of a transition temperature can constrain lattice involvement, provided the compared samples have controlled chemistry and structure. It does not, by itself, identify the complete pairing interaction. This entry distinguishes a mass derivative, a finite comparison between samples and a microscopic explanation.

The classic mercury reports by Maxwell and Reynolds and colleagues, and Fröhlich's early theory paper, are historical starting points. Their bibliographic identities are checked here; their original experimental curves and derivations are not. No mercury exponent is extracted from those metadata records.   

 Mathematical assumptions

For element i, with other masses and specified sample conditions held fixed, define

\alphai=-\frac{\partial\ln Tc}{\partial\ln Mi},\qquad \widehat\alphai=-\frac{\ln(T{c,2}/T{c,1})}{\ln(M{i,2}/M{i,1})}.

The finite estimate averages a slope over the chosen interval; it equals the local derivative only for an appropriate limiting interval or a power law. Use the mean mass implied by measured isotope abundances, not automatically an integer isotope label. A partial coefficient is not the total \alpha{\rm tot}=\sumi\alphai. This sum describes a common logarithmic scaling of all component masses under the same constraints. 

For a harmonic mode with fixed force constant, \omega\propto M^{-1/2}. If the transition scale is proportional to that frequency and all dimensionless interaction parameters remain mass independent, differentiation gives \alpha=1/2. The fixed-parameter condition is essential. A measured deviation challenges that restricted model, not every possible electron–phonon theory. 

An illustrative two-mass optical oscillator makes the distinction concrete. If \omega^2=K(1/M1+1/M2) and Tc\propto\omega, direct differentiation gives

\alpha1=\frac{M2}{2(M1+M2)},\qquad \alpha2=\frac{M1}{2(M1+M2)},\qquad \alpha1+\alpha2=\frac12.

Each partial coefficient can be below one half even in this harmonic construction. These equations are a local illustrative derivation, checked against numerical mass derivatives; they are not a fit to MgB2 or a microscopic pairing calculation.

For uncertainty propagation let N=\ln(T{c,2}/T{c,1}) and D=\ln(M{i,2}/M{i,1}). First-order propagation for \widehat\alpha=-N/D gives

\sigma\alpha^2\simeq\frac{\operatorname{Var}(N)}{D^2}+\frac{N^2\operatorname{Var}(D)}{D^4}-\frac{2N\operatorname{Cov}(N,D)}{D^3}.

This linear approximation requires small uncertainties relative to the resolved mass interval. Shared calibration errors can be correlated; treating all temperatures as independent can misstate the uncertainty. The analytic gradient was checked against finite differences. Those arithmetic checks do not establish experimental precision.

 Experimental criteria

Bud'ko and colleagues report MgB2 isotope samples with magnetic onsets at 40.2 K for boron-10 and 39.2 K for boron-11. They use 25 G, warming after zero-field cooling, and a 2% onset of the low-temperature diamagnetic signal. Heat capacity also shows the shift. Their reported boron coefficient is 0.26\pm0.03, a partial coefficient. Using nominal masses 10 and 11 gives about 0.264 from the stated temperatures; this only checks arithmetic, not enrichment or their error estimate. 

A separate study by Hinks, Claus and Jorgensen measures both components. Its author manuscript reports partial coefficients of 0.30(1) for boron and 0.02(1) for magnesium, with total 0.32(1). Its magnetic protocol uses 1 G and compares extrapolated onset with a 10% criterion. These values belong to that study and must not be assembled from unrelated samples or criteria. The authors explicitly discuss possible impurity effects in their magnesium comparison. 

For a new comparison, report enrichment, composition, structure, defects, preparation history and the exact temperature criterion. Characterize spectral frequency shifts where feasible. Back-exchange can test reversibility, but annealing itself may change the specimen. Repeat controls and uncertainty estimates are needed before assigning a shift exclusively to mass. These are editorial reporting recommendations, not claims that every cited study performed every control.

 Limits and disputes

A small response for one element does not exclude its contribution to a coupled vibrational system. Conversely, a nonzero response does not reconstruct the full electron–phonon spectral function or uniquely determine a mediator. Mass-dependent interactions, anharmonicity and structural changes require explicit models; the sign or size alone cannot settle them. The cited Hinks manuscript discusses alternatives to its own interaction-parameter interpretation. 

Do not merge resistive onset, zero resistance, magnetic screening and a calorimetric transition into one unqualified temperature. The material records below preserve the magnetic criterion actually checked. Pressure and equilibrium classifications not established in the selected passages remain unknown. Comparing isotope coefficients from different studies also requires their sample preparation and systematic uncertainties.

 Discovery implications

Ask which controlled observation would separate a direct mass dependence from a changed sample. Joint measurements of structure, composition, vibrational spectra and independent superconducting probes can narrow the interpretation. Preserve null results and disagreements rather than treating the isotope exponent as a pass/fail label.

A quantitative theory should predict the response of the same observable under the same substitution and constraints. Agreement with one coefficient is a consistency check; a credible explanation must also confront the remaining measurements. These are model-discrimination criteria, not a new material discovery.

entries.title: Superconducting gap: magnitude, nodes and phase
entries.summary: Read gap measurements with their probe and model. Distinguish an excitation scale from evidence for nodes, relative sign or bulk superconductivity.
entries.text:
Scope

A superconducting gap is an energy scale in a specified excitation spectrum. Its magnitude, momentum dependence and relative phase answer different questions. A suppression of spectral weight is not automatically a superconducting gap, and a fitted gap does not automatically define the temperature of bulk superconductivity. This entry organizes observations and model assumptions rather than ranking materials by a single gap ratio.

Specify whether \Delta denotes an order-parameter amplitude, a quasiparticle excitation threshold or a parameter extracted from a broadened spectrum. The relation between these quantities depends on the model. Keep the measured signal, the fit and the inferred state separate; otherwise apparently similar numbers can describe different observables.

 Mathematical assumptions

For a clean, isotropic, single-band weak-coupling BCS model, the quasiparticle spectrum and zero-temperature limiting ratio are

E{\mathbf k}=\sqrt{\xi{\mathbf k}^{\,2}+|\Delta|^2},\qquad \frac{2\Delta0}{kBTc}=2\pi e^{-\gammaE}\simeq3.528.

Here \xi{\mathbf k} is measured from the chemical potential and \gammaE is Euler's constant. The existing BCS entry checks the gap equation and numerical limit. The ratio is not a universal threshold for identifying superconductivity or an interaction. Strong coupling and anisotropy require their own treatment; Carbotte's review abstract describes deviations from simple BCS results without supplying a universal correction.  

With a constant normal density of states Nn and the same spin convention in numerator and denominator, the ideal normalized density of states at positive excitation energy is

\frac{Ns(E)}{Nn}=\begin{cases}0,&0\le E<|\Delta|,\\ E/\sqrt{E^2-|\Delta|^2},&E>|\Delta|.\end{cases}

The factor above the edge follows from the change of variable E=\sqrt{\xi^2+|\Delta|^2} with the usual Bogoliubov spectral weights. The ideal edge is singular but integrable. A local numerical check integrates it up to a finite energy and recovers the corresponding normal-state \xi interval. The check assumes no lifetime broadening, gap anisotropy or experimental convolution. 

In this magnitude-only model, replacing a gap by its negative leaves the excitation energies unchanged. Likewise, independently summing two uncoupled spectral contributions cannot recover their relative sign. This is a limited counterexample to inferring phase from a gap magnitude; it does not say that every interference-sensitive spectrum is phase blind.

 Experimental criteria

Use the following as a reporting map adapted from the pinned chapter. Each interpretation needs the stated model and a sample-specific source; these rows do not certify any material dataset.

| Probe | Recorded quantity | What must be controlled |
|---|---|---|
| Tunneling or STS | Differential conductance versus bias | Tip and sample spectra, thermal/instrumental broadening, matrix elements and surface variation |
| ARPES | Momentum-resolved photoemission intensity | Occupation, resolution, matrix elements and surface state; a leading edge is not automatically a gap amplitude |
| Optical or THz spectroscopy | Frequency-dependent electrodynamic response | Scattering, multiple bands and the model linking absorption to an excitation threshold |
| Heat capacity | Entropy and bulk excitation contribution | Lattice/magnetic backgrounds and normalization; no direct phase measurement |
| Penetration depth or thermal transport | Low-energy electromagnetic or heat response | Disorder, nonlocality, background and multiple excitation channels |
| Andreev or point-contact spectroscopy | Interface current and conductance | Barrier transparency, heating, contact regime and channel mixing |

A tunnel conductance resembles the sample density of states only with suitable assumptions about the counterelectrode and tunneling matrix element, and after accounting for the thermal convolution. Do not identify every conductance peak with \Delta. Photoemission and thermodynamic measurements constrain different aspects of the state; the selected review discusses why magnitude-sensitive probes alone do not measure the relative phase. 

Hardy and colleagues report a strong linear term in the penetration-depth change of YBa2Cu3O6.95 single crystals over approximately 3–25 K using a 900 MHz resonator. This is evidence relevant to low-energy excitations under their sample conditions, not a direct measurement of gap phase. The present check covers the publisher abstract. 

By contrast, Tsuei and Kirtley use scanning SQUID measurements of NCCO/PCCO tricrystals to test phase-sensitive predictions. Their designed frustrated geometry produces a half-flux signal, while two unfrustrated NCCO geometries serve as controls. The inference depends on junction geometry and the associated model, not merely on observing a spectral dip. Selected author-manuscript passages and the control description were checked; the image fits were not independently reproduced. 

 Limits and disputes

Nodes, relative sign and topology are distinct. A low-temperature power law can constrain low-energy excitations without uniquely selecting a pairing representation. A fully open gap on each Fermi-surface sheet can coexist with a relative sign change between sheets. Disorder and sample inhomogeneity must be considered before translating a temperature dependence into a symmetry assignment. 

A zero-bias feature alone is not a unique topology test. Identify its field, temperature, position and junction dependence, then compare explicit alternative models. Likewise, a spectroscopic gap-closing temperature must not silently replace a resistive or thermodynamic Tc in a gap ratio. These are inference and reporting limits, not a claim that one alternative explains every observed feature.

Choi and colleagues' MgB2 result is an anisotropic Eliashberg calculation of distinct band-dependent gap scales. Treat those calculated gaps as theory and compare them with separately identified measurements. The pinned chapter's DOI was mismatched; the correct source is nature00898. That correction does not validate a universal multiband gap ratio or independently reproduce the calculation. 

 Discovery implications

Record the specimen, pressure or strain, temperature criterion, spectral resolution, fit model and uncertainty together. Compare probes on the same or demonstrably comparable specimens. A disagreement can expose a surface effect, background assumption or a second energy scale; it should remain visible until tested.

A useful next measurement distinguishes competing interpretations. Establish which observation would separate a change of magnitude from a change of phase, and which control would rule out a contact artifact or another ordered state. Gap measurements constrain models; they do not replace a complete evidence chain for superconductivity.

entries.title: Critical fields: thermodynamic, orbital and Pauli scales
entries.summary: Distinguish Hc, Hc1 and Hc2, compare orbital and spin limits, and keep experimental field criteria attached to their conditions.
entries.text:
Scope

A critical field needs a physical definition. The thermodynamic field Hc represents the zero-field condensation-energy density, fn-fs=\mu0Hc^2/2. This energy scale exists for both type-I and type-II superconductors; it is not generally the field at which a type-II sample becomes normal. In the ideal bulk type-II description, H{c1} marks the equilibrium onset of the mixed state and H{c2} its upper boundary. The vortex construction distinguishes those boundaries from one thermodynamic energy scale. 

Here H is magnetic field strength in amperes per metre, while B and \mu0H are expressed in tesla. Inside matter, B=\mu0(H+M); replacing B by \mu0H requires a stated magnetization approximation. An applied-field value, an internal field and a flux density must not silently share the same symbol. The formulas below use SI conventions, rather than copying Gaussian-unit factors from historical papers.

 Mathematical assumptions

For a bulk, isotropic, single-component Ginzburg–Landau model near Tc, neglecting paramagnetic pair breaking, linearization gives the orbital result


B{c2}^{\mathrm{orb}}=\frac{\Phi0}{2\pi\xi^2},\qquad
\Phi0=\frac{h}{2e},\qquad
\kappa=\frac{\lambda}{\xi}.


The usual \mu0H{c2}^{\mathrm{orb}} notation uses B\simeq\mu0H near this continuous boundary when normal-state magnetic response is negligible. In the same model, H{c2}^{\mathrm{orb}}=\sqrt{2}\kappa Hc. The GL coherence length \xi and penetration depth \lambda are evaluated at the same temperature. They are not interchangeable with every microscopic pair-size or fitted length. The isotropic GL type-II boundary is \kappa=1/\sqrt{2}. 

A useful independent check follows from the linearized kinetic operator: the lowest Landau-level energy of a pair with charge magnitude 2e is \hbar(2e)B/(2m^\ast). Equating it to |\alpha|, with \xi^2=\hbar^2/(2m^\ast|\alpha|), gives the flux-over-area expression above. This is a model derivation, not a measured field or an all-temperature interpolation.

For a separate, purely paramagnetic comparison at zero temperature, take an isotropic weak-coupling singlet with g=2, negligible spin susceptibility in the paired state, no orbital cost and no competing modulated state. Equating its condensation energy to the normal-state polarization-energy gain gives


BP=\frac{\Delta0}{\sqrt{2}\muB},\qquad
\frac{BP}{Tc}=\frac{\pi e^{-\gamma}kB}{\sqrt{2}\muB}
\simeq 1.86\;\mathrm{T\,K^{-1}}.


This is the Clogston–Chandrasekhar reference scale. The commonly quoted 1.84\;\mathrm{T\,K^{-1}} uses rounded weak-coupling gap constants; neither coefficient is an exact universal experimental bound. The numerical value here uses the same modern weak-coupling gap convention as the BCS entry. The energy comparison is supported by the cited perspective; the original Clogston paper's identity is checked, but its full text was not available in this review.   

 Experimental criteria

Report the probe and the rule used to locate a field line. Resistance onset, a stated percentage of the normal-state resistance and a voltage-resolution-limited zero need not coincide. Neither a magnetic irreversibility line nor a first flux-entry signal should automatically be renamed H{c2} or equilibrium H{c1}. Demagnetizing geometry, surface barriers, vortex motion, pinning and inhomogeneous current paths can affect the observed signal.

Record temperature, field orientation and angular uncertainty, sample geometry, pressure where relevant, current density, sweep direction and rate, and the normal-state baseline. Compare transport with an appropriate bulk thermodynamic or magnetic measurement on comparable specimens. Preserve hysteresis and transition widths instead of choosing the most favorable boundary. These are measurement-reporting requirements from the pinned chapter, not a claim that each possible artifact is present in a particular sample.

 Limits and disputes

Werthamer–Helfand–Hohenberg theory treats orbital and spin effects within a specified microscopic approximation, including spin–orbit impurity scattering. Its publisher abstract explicitly notes that such scattering counteracts paramagnetic limiting. A fitted WHH curve therefore needs its dirty-limit, spin and scattering assumptions; merely naming the fit does not establish them. This entry's WHH check is abstract-scoped. 

Multiband structure also changes extrapolation. Gurevich's dirty two-gap model allows H{c2}(T) shapes controlled by different intraband diffusivities, including deviations from the one-gap slope estimate near Tc. That calculation is a counterexample to treating a one-band extrapolation coefficient as universal. It does not validate an arbitrary multiband fit or supply a field value for an unmeasured sample. 

Exceeding the simple Pauli estimate does not uniquely identify triplet pairing. The spin response and spin–orbit energy scales may differ from the assumed reference model; the cited Ising-superconductivity perspective discusses a concrete route to a strongly anisotropic paramagnetic response. Orbital and spin limitations must be treated together when both matter. No material-specific critical-field record or pairing assignment is introduced here. 

 Discovery implications

Use a field measurement to discriminate between declared models. First decide whether the observation concerns an equilibrium boundary, vortex dynamics or a transport threshold. Then test orientation and temperature dependence over a range where the model applies. Retain the fitting window, parameter uncertainty and alternative descriptions, particularly when extrapolating far below the measured temperatures.

A high critical field may motivate further study, but a useful discovery argument identifies which assumption failed and which new observable could distinguish the remaining explanations. Material comparisons should keep pressure, field direction and criterion attached to each value. A large fitted field alone establishes neither a microscopic pairing mediator nor topology. This is an editorial evaluation protocol; it is not a newly verified experimental result.

entries.title: Critical current: criteria, geometry and pinning
entries.summary: Compare transport, magnetization and depairing limits with their field, time scale and area convention. Preserve measurement conditions before comparing conductor performance.
entries.text:
Scope

Critical current is a limit defined for a specimen, measurement protocol and operating conditions. Transport measurements use a voltage or electric-field criterion; magnetization measurements infer a current through a model; the depairing current describes loss of stability of a superconducting state within a specified theory. These quantities must not share an unlabeled performance ranking.

Blatter and colleagues explicitly distinguish depinning and depairing current densities in their review abstract. Pinning, thermal fluctuations and vortex motion affect practical current transport. A measured threshold can instead be limited by weak connections or heating; its mechanism requires evidence beyond the value of the current itself. 

 Mathematical assumptions

For voltage taps separated by length L, define the mean longitudinal electric-field criterion Ec=Vc/L. Using the same measured Ic, distinguish the nominal superconducting cross-section As from the entire conductor area At:

Jc=\frac{Ic}{As},\qquad Je=\frac{Ic}{At}=fJc,\qquad f=\frac{As}{At}.

Here Je is an engineering current density for the stated whole-conductor area. Nominal superconducting area does not resolve nonuniform current paths or pores. A different definition of non-copper area, filament area or cable area requires a different label. These identities compare area conventions; they do not correct a damaged conductor or infer intrinsic microscopic current density.

A simple sensitivity calculation illustrates why the criterion matters. If a measured interval is modeled by E=E0(J/J0)^n with positive constant n, changing the criterion by a factor r changes the inferred current by r^{1/n}. For n=20, a tenfold criterion change gives a factor of about 1.122. This is an illustrative power-law calculation, not a measured exponent or a universal transport law.

The magnetic force density is the vector product \mathbf F=\mathbf J\times\mathbf B. For current perpendicular to the induction, its magnitude at the threshold becomes Fp=JcB if a static pinning-force balance is the applicable model. In SI units this is N/m³; resistive heating instead has power density \mathbf E\cdot\mathbf J in W/m³. A parallel configuration has no force from this cross product. Replacing B by \mu0H requires an additional approximation, especially near self-field conditions.

For an explicit geometry check, take an infinite slab of full thickness 2a, field parallel to its faces, constant Jc and fully developed opposite critical-state branches. Neglect demagnetization, reversible magnetization and creep. Ampere's law gives |dB/dx|=\mu0Jc. With x measured across the thickness, the ideal branch profiles are B\pm(x)=\mu0[Ha\pm Jc(a-|x|)]. Their spatial averages give

M\pm=\pm\frac{Jca}{2},\qquad \Delta M=M+-M-=Jca,\qquad Jc=\frac{\Delta M}{a}.

\Delta M is the full vertical loop width in A/m; a is the half-thickness in metres. Numerically integrating these stated profiles verifies the factor and dimensions. This is a local derivation under ideal assumptions, not a reanalysis of Bean's original data. Bean's 1962 paper is the historical source; its full text was not available in this check. Do not transfer this slab expression to arbitrary films, cylinders, partial penetration or field-dependent Jc. 

 Experimental criteria

Keep enough information to reconstruct both the measured threshold and the conversion to a current density. The following is an editorial reporting guide, not a table of certified material records.

| Measurement | Record with the result | Interpretation boundary |
|---|---|---|
| Transport | Temperature, field magnitude and orientation, voltage-tap spacing, electric-field criterion, current ramp or pulse duration, duty cycle, area convention | Contact heating, current sharing and voltage offsets can change the inferred threshold |
| Magnetization | Magnetic moment, volume, dimensions, field history, sweep rate, elapsed time and background subtraction | Conversion to current requires a geometry and critical-state model |
| Conductor or cable | Superconducting fraction, whole-conductor area, length, strain and thermal stabilization | Layer current density and engineering current density answer different questions |
| Depairing model | Model, temperature regime, geometry and stability assumptions | A calculated instability is not automatically the measured transport limit |

MacManus-Driscoll and colleagues studied YBCO films grown with BaZrO3 added to the target. Their selected manuscript passages report improved in-field transport at 75.5 K, despite lower transition temperature or self-field current in some samples. The rotated field remained perpendicular to current. This comparison illustrates distinct performance measures, not proof of a different pairing mechanism. No electric-field criterion was extracted here, so no numerical current record is tabulated. 

Larbalestier and colleagues' 2014 paper is a primary Bi-2212 round-wire study, not a general engineering review. Its earlier author manuscript distinguishes whole-conductor Je from superconducting-area Jc and compares short specimens with a demonstration coil. This entry uses that distinction without importing a cross-family ranking; the final published dataset and all measurement criteria were not independently re-extracted. 

 Limits and disputes

An irreversible magnetic response and the upper critical field are different observables. A loss of measurable hysteresis or a transport threshold need not locate the destruction of superconductivity. Report the criterion, time scale and field history rather than silently equating an irreversibility line with H{c2}. Thermally activated creep is one reason different observation times can yield different apparent current limits. 

A fitted pinning-curve exponent or angular peak does not uniquely identify a defect. Compare microscopy, processing controls and temperature/angle dependence. In the checked YBCO manuscript, the detailed composition of the small second-phase particles is not conclusively established; describing every particle as chemically proven BaZrO3 would overstate the evidence. 

 Discovery implications

Separate a better transport path, stronger pinning, a larger superconducting fraction and a higher depairing limit as distinct hypotheses. Compare controlled specimens under matched conditions before assigning an improvement to a microscopic mechanism. A gain in current-carrying performance does not by itself demonstrate higher Tc, a new pairing interaction or a new superconducting phase.

Preserve the measured signal, uncertainty and analysis conventions together. If the voltage criterion, geometry or thermal history is unavailable, retain that gap in the record. A useful follow-up is the measurement that discriminates between the competing limits, rather than another unsupported performance ranking.

entries.text:
Scope

Linear-temperature resistivity describes a measured dependence over a specified range. The fit \rho(T)=\rho0+AT needs a sample, current direction, field, temperature interval and residuals. A straight-looking trace is not by itself evidence for a quantum critical point, a universal lifetime or a pairing interaction. This entry treats transport phenomenology; the linked Planckian entry discusses lifetime interpretations.

Separate a finite-field normal state, the region affected by superconducting fluctuations, and a higher-temperature regime that may have different scattering. Martin and colleagues' Bi-based crystal abstract reports strongly anisotropic transport; an in-plane trend is not an isotropic resistivity law. 

 Mathematical assumptions

A least-squares slope depends on both the model and the sampled window. For exact synthetic data \rho=r0+aT+bT^2, equally weighted temperatures symmetric about \bar T give

A{\mathrm{fit}}=a+2b\bar T.

This follows by inserting the quadratic into \operatorname{cov}(T,\rho)/\operatorname{var}(T). A narrower interval can hide curvature while changing the inferred slope. Independent synthetic fits confirm this counterexample; they are not fits to any material. Experimental model comparison also needs uncertainties, correlations and a justified treatment of residuals.

For a single isotropic Drude channel with temperature-independent carrier density n and mass m^, an inelastic pole relaxation rate \gamma=\alpha kBT/\hbar gives A=\alpha m^kB/(ne^2\hbar). Thus a slope fixes \alpha only after the carrier parameters and response model are specified. If those parameters change with temperature, differentiating resistivity produces additional terms. This conditional connection underlies the selected Legros analysis. 

For a circular, parabolic two-dimensional band with total degeneracy g, use total sheet density n{2D}=gkF^2/(4\pi) and kBTF=\hbar^2kF^2/(2m^). The preceding Drude model then yields

A{\square}TF=\frac{\alpha h}{g e^2}.

The familiar factor of two corresponds to g=2, not an arbitrary multiband system. A bulk slope converted per conducting plane uses A{\square}=A/d with the stated effective plane spacing d. Independent occupied-disk and algebra checks cover g=1,2,4; neither degeneracy nor a mass should be transferred between materials without justification.

Parallel channels add conductivities. As an independent scalar, zero-field example, let r(T)=r0+aT>0 describe one channel and let \sigmab\ge0 be a constant background conductivity in matching units. Then

\rho{\mathrm{tot}}=\frac{r(T)}{1+\sigmab r(T)},\qquad\frac{d\rho{\mathrm{tot}}}{dT}=\frac{a}{[1+\sigmab r(T)]^2}.

The total slope is generally temperature dependent even though the first channel's resistance is exactly linear. Nine numerical derivative checks verify this model. It is not a multiband fit; in magnetic field, conductivity tensors must be added before inversion. Adding scattering mechanisms within one channel is a different assumption from adding parallel conductivities.

 Experimental criteria

Legros and colleagues' earlier manuscript measures a Bi2212 film with nominal hole doping 0.23 in pulsed fields. Its 55 T trace and magnetoresistance-corrected, extrapolated zero-field curve are distinct datasets. The analysis estimates carrier parameters and geometric uncertainty; the checked passages do not turn its interpretation into a model-independent universal bound. 

Cao and colleagues measure four-probe transport in gated twisted bilayer graphene. Their linear regime depends on filling and a crossover temperature. The operational scattering coefficient uses density and mass from low-temperature quantum oscillations; those assumptions matter when interpreting higher-temperature transport. The selected passages do not establish one shared microscopic mechanism across material families. 

Romero and colleagues' earlier manuscript studies two 100 nm FeTe1-xSex films, x = 0.45 and 0.35, over 0.2–3 THz. Its narrow-channel fits use 20–40 K and report coefficients 3.02 and 2.42 in \Gamma=\Gamma0+\alpha kBT/h. These are channel-specific fit results, not coefficients of the total DC resistivity. 

Record the raw voltage/current or conductivity data, geometry, composition, field direction, fit interval and uncertainty model. Identify excluded transition regions and test alternative fit windows and curvature. A successful fit does not establish that its parameters are uniquely identifiable. Normal-state measurement temperatures remain separate from superconducting transition temperatures in the records below.

 Limits and disputes

Frequency conventions can create a factor-of-2\pi error. For a Drude denominator \Gamma-i\nu with ordinary frequency \nu, the corresponding pole rate is \gamma=1/\tau=2\pi\Gamma in a denominator \gamma-i\omega, where \omega=2\pi\nu. Consequently \Gamma=\alpha kBT/h converts to \gamma=\alpha kBT/\hbar. State the denominator and linewidth convention before comparing coefficients. This is a convention check, not a new measurement of a lifetime.

A shared temperature exponent does not identify a unique microscopic interaction. Drude transport, optical fits and single-particle lifetimes measure or infer different quantities. Extrapolating carrier parameters, suppressing superconductivity by field, or neglecting a parallel channel can affect an inferred coefficient. Report these choices alongside any claimed universality rather than treating the fit exponent as a proof.

Cooper's LSCO study and Bruin's cross-metal comparison remain bibliographic starting points here. Their complete datasets and numerical conclusions have not been reanalyzed in this entry. Selected manuscript checks above also leave final-version comparison and full uncertainty reproduction open.  

 Discovery implications

Use linear-T transport to organize experiments, not to rank superconductors or predict a transition temperature by itself. A stronger comparison holds sample state, probe definition and fitting procedure fixed, then asks whether independent optical, thermodynamic or quantum-oscillation information supports the same parameter interpretation. Retain counterexamples and failed fits; correlation with superconductivity does not identify its cause.

entries.title: Andreev reflection: interface transport and model limits
entries.summary: Understand electron–hole conversion, barrier-dependent conductance and thermal smearing. Keep contact assumptions separate from claims about bulk symmetry or topology.

entries.text:
Scope

Andreev reflection converts an electron-like excitation in a normal conductor into a reflected hole-like excitation at a superconducting interface. In the conventional subgap process, charge of magnitude 2e enters the condensate. Andreev's original calculation treats a slowly varying excitation near the Fermi surface; the selected scan shows subgap evanescence and reversal of velocity. Retroreflection is an approximation with a specified band and energy regime, not a universal trajectory rule. 

This is an interface probe. Conductance depends on the contact as well as the superconducting state, so a fitted gap scale or an enhanced subgap signal is not automatically a measurement of bulk pairing symmetry. Keep interface scattering, normal-state background and sample conditions attached to an interpretation.

 Mathematical assumptions

For one incident channel, let A(E) and B(E) be Andreev and normal reflection probabilities with consistent flux normalization. The charge-conductance weight is 1+A-B. Under purely subgap reflection, probability conservation gives A+B=1, hence the weight is 2A. A factor of two in this ideal charge conversion does not imply that every measured junction has twice its normal-state conductance.

The original BTK abstract describes a tunable interface barrier. To check an explicit limit independently, take a spin-degenerate, single-channel, time-reversal-symmetric normal barrier of transmission \mathcal T, separated from an ideal conventional s-wave Andreev reflector. At zero energy the round-trip Andreev phase is -1, giving

A(0)=\left(\frac{\mathcal T}{2-\mathcal T}\right)^2,\qquad \frac{G{NS}}{GN}=\frac{2\mathcal T}{(2-\mathcal T)^2}.

For a one-dimensional delta barrier with matched velocities, define Z so that \mathcal T=1/(1+Z^2). Summing coherent electron–hole round trips gives A(0)=1/(1+2Z^2)^2. The transparent limit has conductance ratio two; the tunnel limit is suppressed. Independent complex-amplitude sums check twelve barrier/energy cases. This is an ideal scattering check, not a reanalysis of BTK's full finite-bias treatment. 

Beenakker's later lectures give, at zero temperature, bias and magnetic field, G{NS}=(4e^2/h)\sumn\mathcal Tn^2/(2-\mathcal Tn)^2 and GN=(2e^2/h)\sumn\mathcal Tn. These are two-terminal formulas for the stated coherent NS model, with normal scattering separated from the ideal superconducting boundary. The original 1992 paper is retained separately at abstract scope.  

Equal normal conductance does not determine the superconducting conductance. For example, transmission sets (1,0) and (1/2,1/2) have the same sum but different sums of \mathcal Tn^2/(2-\mathcal Tn)^2. This independent counterexample explains why a contact resistance alone cannot specify a multichannel junction.

For an elastic spectrum g0(E) whose temperature dependence is held fixed, thermal smearing is a convolution with the Fermi derivative:

G(V,T)=\int dE\,g0(E)\frac{\operatorname{sech}^2[(E-eV)/(2kBT)]}{4kBT}.

The kernel integrates to one and preserves a constant conductance. Three numerical checks compare the convolution to the derivative of its corresponding current integral. The check uses a synthetic smooth spectrum, not a BTK fit. A temperature-dependent gap, bias-dependent barrier, nonequilibrium distribution or heating requires additional modeling; arbitrary lifetime broadening is not equivalent to thermal convolution.

 Experimental criteria

Blonder and Tinkham's 1983 experimental abstract reports Cu-Nb point contacts spanning metallic to tunneling behavior and agreement with the model over a range of contact resistances. This entry checks that qualitative observation only. Contact dimensions, individual spectra and parameter uncertainties remain unverified here; no transition temperature is extracted. 

Report contact preparation, normal-state resistance, wiring, crystal direction, current or excitation amplitude, field and temperature. Compare contact dimensions with mean free path and coherence length before choosing a ballistic or diffusive description. Repeat contacts and test heating and critical-current artifacts. Preserve the background normalization and its uncertainty; these are editorial requirements for assessing a claim, not one universally valid apparatus recipe.

A constant series resistance Rs gives G{\mathrm{meas}}=G{\mathrm{int}}/(1+RsG{\mathrm{int}}) when the internal response is differentiated consistently. Ignoring it can change an apparent enhancement or fitted transparency. This circuit identity assumes the series element is bias independent; it does not describe thermal feedback or nonlinear leads.

 Limits and disputes

Asano, Tanaka and Kashiwaya's theoretical abstract associates a sign-changing pair potential with zero-energy surface states and a zero-bias conductance peak. This is a model result about a surface, not a new experimental proof of bulk symmetry. The broad Kashiwaya–Tanaka review is retained as a bibliographic pointer; its detailed calculations have not been checked here.  

A peak alone does not establish a Majorana mode, spin-triplet pairing or a unique mechanism. Model comparison should address ordinary bound states and junction effects, and test the predicted orientation, field, temperature and spatial dependence. Surface roughness and mixed trajectories can change the inference. A phase-sensitive experiment and a local conductance spectrum answer different questions.

 Discovery implications

Use interface spectroscopy to constrain candidate gap and scattering models, then seek independent bulk and phase-sensitive evidence. Report competing parameter sets and failed alternatives alongside a best fit. A good fit can support consistency with a model while leaving parameter uniqueness and microscopic causation unresolved. Preserve that distinction in both prose and machine-readable records.

entries.title: BCS theory: the weak-coupling baseline
entries.summary: Cooper pairing, the gap equation and the 3.528 gap ratio, with the assumptions that make these useful model benchmarks rather than universal material rules.
entries.text:
Scope

BCS theory provides a microscopic pairing framework and a useful weak-coupling reference point. This article concerns its equilibrium, single-band, isotropic implementation with a smooth density of states and an effective attraction near the Fermi surface. Those assumptions define a model, not a classification of every superconductor. Agreement with one numerical ratio does not uniquely identify a pairing interaction. 

The Cooper problem asks what happens when two electrons interact above an otherwise inert, filled Fermi sea. In the idealized attractive-shell model, a bound pair exists below the two-particle continuum for arbitrarily weak net attraction. The filled sea and its excluded states are essential to this result. It is not a claim that every attractive potential binds two isolated electrons in vacuum, nor is the two-electron calculation alone a construction of the finite-density superconducting state. 

 Mathematical assumptions

Write the attractive matrix element as -V, with V>0. Let N(0) count states of one spin per unit energy, using the same volume normalization as V, so \lambda=N(0)V is dimensionless. The energy cutoff is Ec=\hbar\omegac, where \omegac is an angular frequency. With \xi measured relative to the chemical potential, the excitation spectrum and gap equation are


E(\xi)=\sqrt{\xi^2+|\Delta|^2},



1=\lambda\int0^{Ec}\frac{\tanh[E(\xi)/(2kBT)]}{E(\xi)}\,d\xi.


The positive-energy integral already accounts for the symmetric negative-energy interval in the momentum-sum formulation. Inserting a two-spin density of states without changing the prefactor doubles the effective coupling. At zero temperature this model gives \Delta0=Ec/\sinh(1/\lambda). For \lambda\ll1, the usual limiting forms are


kBTc\simeq\frac{2e^\gamma}{\pi}Ec e^{-1/\lambda},



\frac{2\Delta0}{kBTc}\simeq2\pi e^{-\gamma}\simeq3.528.


Here \gamma is the Euler–Mascheroni constant; 2e^\gamma/\pi\simeq1.134. These are model results, not a measured transition temperature. We use modern \Delta notation for the single-quasiparticle threshold; creating two quasiparticles costs at least 2\Delta in this idealized spectrum. The original paper used different notation and rounded numerical estimates. 

 Experimental criteria

A useful comparison needs a gap measurement and a separately specified superconducting transition criterion on a comparable sample. Report whether the measured quantity is a single-particle threshold, a pair-breaking energy or a fitted spectral parameter. State temperature, magnetic field, sample composition and uncertainty before calculating a gap ratio. A peak separation must not silently be substituted for \Delta0.

Then compare more than one observable: the temperature evolution of the gap, electronic thermodynamics and magnetic response constrain different aspects of the state. Distinguish a consistency test of the isotropic weak-coupling model from evidence for a particular microscopic mediator. No sample-specific Tc or gap value is added to the material-comparison catalogue by this theoretical article. 

 Limits and disputes

The general pairing construction should not be equated with a universal weak-coupling phonon mechanism. A frequency-dependent interaction, several coupled bands, an anisotropic gap or a rapidly varying density of states requires a more suitable equation. Phase fluctuations can also separate a pairing scale from the temperature at which long-range or quasi-long-range coherence develops. The simple gap equation above does not calculate that fluctuation problem.

The familiar isotope exponent -d\ln Tc/d\ln M=1/2 follows only if the cutoff has harmonic mass scaling and the remaining effective parameters are mass-independent. Changes in structure or coupling invalidate that inference. Likewise, a nonstandard gap ratio can motivate tests of stronger coupling or anisotropy; it does not, by itself, prove a named alternative mechanism. These applicability cautions follow the scope of the pinned B1 source chapter and are not new experimental findings. 

 Discovery implications

Use BCS as a controlled baseline: define the band model, interaction window and normalization before fitting. Check that the inferred scales fit within the regime assumed by the calculation, rather than extrapolating an exponential formula into a flat-band or low-density regime. Compare alternative explanations using measurements that distinguish them. In particular, finding a Cooper instability is a starting point for a many-body theory, not the final demonstration of a material's phase coherence or pairing mediator. 

A productive research record should retain which assumption failed, which observation exposed the failure and which additional measurement could decide between the remaining models. This is editorial guidance for using the baseline, not a claim of an experimentally established route to higher Tc.

entries.text:
Scope

Hund coupling is an intra-atomic exchange interaction that changes the energies and fluctuations of multiorbital electrons. It can organize a correlated metallic state without identifying the interaction that produces superconductivity. Orbital-dependent masses, slow screening and local moments are normal-state constraints on a pairing theory; they do not specify its Cooper-channel eigenfunction.

The de' Medici–Mravlje–Georges three-orbital calculation illustrates a filling-dependent distinction. For two electrons, increasing Hund coupling can reduce quasiparticle coherence while moving the Mott threshold to stronger repulsion. The corresponding singly occupied and half-filled cases behave differently. This is the Janus effect in a specified model, not a universal monotonic relation between Hund coupling and transition temperature. 

 Mathematical assumptions

Specify the correlated orbitals, their crystal-field energies and the interaction convention. In the Kanamori convention used here, U penalizes opposite spins in one orbital, U' couples opposite spins in different orbitals, and U'-J couples parallel spins in different orbitals. Spin-flip and pair-hopping amplitudes are retained. For the usual degenerate-shell reduction with both amplitudes equal to J, we impose U'=U-2J. The review distinguishes this assumption from more general rotationally invariant interactions; the relation cannot be inferred from spin symmetry alone. 

An independent finite-atom check constructs the full Fock-space Hamiltonian, including fermionic signs, for two and three orbitals. There is no hopping between atoms, bath or spin-orbit coupling. With two electrons and positive J, the two-orbital eigenvalues and degeneracies are

E=U-3J\ (3),\qquad U-J\ (2),\qquad U+J\ (1).

The lowest triplet is threefold degenerate. Keeping density interactions alone leaves only two states at this lowest energy and shifts the opposite-spin combination. It therefore changes the spin multiplet, even when the parameters retain the same names. Direct diagonalizations at three parameter sets verify this distinction; the omission is not a harmless numerical shortcut.

With three degenerate orbitals, the two-electron sector instead has energies U-3J, U-J and U+2J, with degeneracies 9, 5 and 1. Counting all 15 states checks that spin and orbital multiplicities have both been included. These finite spectra provide a reproducible convention test before a lattice calculation; they are not a prediction of quasiparticle coherence.

Define the atomic charge-addition gap using ground-state energies at fixed electron number:

\Delta{\mathrm{at}}(N)=E0(N+1)+E0(N-1)-2E0(N).

For the three-orbital model at the tested repulsive parameters, direct diagonalization gives \Delta{\mathrm{at}}(1)=\Delta{\mathrm{at}}(2)=U-3J, but \Delta{\mathrm{at}}(3)=U+2J. Nine numerical charge-gap checks reproduce these expressions. The half-filled shell responds differently to exchange. A finite atomic addition gap is neither a superconducting excitation gap nor a solid's critical interaction: bandwidth, hybridization and self-consistency are missing. The original Janus paper also separates this atomic argument from the low-coherence metallic regime. 

Crystal-field splitting provides a second independent illustration. Put two orbital energies at -\delta/2 and +\delta/2, keep two electrons, and retain pair hopping. The mixed doubly occupied singlet has energy U-\sqrt{\delta^2+J^2}, while the triplet has energy U-3J. Four matrix checks confirm a crossing at |\delta|=\sqrt8J. For U=6, J=1 and \delta=4 in arbitrary energy units, the singlet is lower despite positive Hund coupling. This example excludes any unconditional statement that Hund exchange guarantees a high-spin ground state in a crystal.

 Experimental criteria

Separate an orbital-resolved theoretical self-energy from a measured band dispersion or a thermodynamic sum over bands. State the temperature, field, reference band calculation and fitting window. A mass comparison can depend on the chosen correlated subspace and ligand hybridization; one universal enhancement factor should not be transferred between iron compounds, ruthenates and nickelates.

Hardy and colleagues studied KFe2As2 using resistivity, calorimetry, thermal expansion and susceptibility. Their accepted manuscript reports a zero-field heat-capacity transition at 3.4 K and a 5.5 T, c-axis comparison for the normal-state curve. It warns that a large residual-resistivity ratio can reflect strong high-temperature scattering rather than exceptionally few defects. The normal-state coherence interpretation and the superconducting transition are separate observations; neither constitutes a direct measurement of a unique pairing interaction. Selected manuscript pages were checked, not the full raw data. 

Yin, Haule and Kotliar compared iron compounds with DFT+DMFT while fixing the local interaction matrix. Their analysis connects orbital differentiation to structure and describes cancellation between direct and ligand-mediated hopping for the xy orbital. These are material calculations with explicit approximations. The paper's proposed structural optimization for superconductivity remains an inference, not an experimental demonstration that maximizing Hund coupling raises Tc. 

 Limits and disputes

The Yin paper has a published erratum: the material label in Figures 1 and 2 is BaFe2As2, replacing the original BaFe2Se2 label. The corrected publisher PDF and appended erratum were checked, including a visual inspection of the correction. Preserve this identity when reusing the comparison.  

A reduced bare triplet interaction U-3J can remain positive. In all three repulsive parameter sets checked above it does. Lowering one atomic energy relative to another does not demonstrate an attractive effective interaction between low-energy quasiparticles. A pairing calculation must include the relevant momentum, frequency, spin and orbital structure, along with normal-state renormalization and competing orders.

Spin freezing describes a dynamical regime over specified temperatures and timescales; it must not automatically be relabeled a zero-temperature magnetic phase. The finite-atom checks here cannot establish that regime because they contain no environment or relaxation process. Full final-version comparison, material-specific vertex calculations and independent experimental replication remain outside this entry's completed review.

A 2026 bilayer-nickelate calculation illustrates why the pairing problem must be evaluated separately. Maier and colleagues analyze a two-orbital Hubbard–Hund model with a cluster method. Its two-site instability is near 140 K, while the authors infer a scale around 100 K for the large-system model. Neither is a measured material Tc. The two-site cluster omits spatial phase fluctuations; larger clusters encounter a low-temperature fermion sign problem. These limitations bound the proposed interlayer pairing interpretation. 

 Discovery implications

Vary filling, crystal-field splitting or structure within a clearly specified model, and compare normal-state predictions against multiple probes before solving the pairing problem. Record which interaction terms and vertex corrections are retained. Test whether a candidate enhancement survives reduced coherence and competing magnetism. Report the resulting pairing eigenfunction and its assumptions rather than ranking materials by J or mass alone.
