entries.title: Topological superconductivity
entries.summary: Connect symmetry, bulk invariants and boundary evidence while separating Majorana model constructions, experimental readout and unresolved identification.
entries.text:
Scope

Topological superconductivity describes a paired state's quasiparticle structure under specified dimensionality, symmetry and gap conditions. It does not name an independent pairing interaction. This entry concentrates on fully gapped Bogoliubov–de Gennes (BdG) descriptions; topology of nodal superconductors requires a different invariant and boundary analysis. The noninteracting/BdG classification is not, by itself, a complete classification of interacting phases. 

Read and Green distinguish weak and strong pairing in a specified two-dimensional spinless p-wave model. This establishes a theoretical phase distinction, not a classification of every material with an unusual tunnelling spectrum. A material claim needs a superconducting state compatible with the proposed invariant and the relevant boundary geometry. 

 Mathematical assumptions

For a spinless chain, take positive nearest-neighbour hopping t, real pairing \Delta, chemical potential \mu and unit lattice spacing. One Nambu convention gives

H(k)=(-\mu-2t\cos k)\tauz+2\Delta\sin k\,\tauy,\qquad E\pm(k)=\pm\sqrt{(\mu+2t\cos k)^2+4\Delta^2\sin^2 k}.

The bulk is gapped for nonzero \Delta away from |\mu|=2t. The particle-hole-protected parity index is Q=\operatorname{sgn}(\mu^2-4t^2): Q=-1 identifies the nontrivial region. The real-parameter chain also has an additional effective time-reversal symmetry; retaining that symmetry gives the finer BDI classification. Using its class-D parity does not claim that its additional symmetry is absent. These are ideal mean-field assumptions, not a determination of an experimental device's parameters.  

An independent finite-matrix check constructs the hopping and antisymmetric pairing blocks directly. Five periodic eight-site spectra agree with the analytic energies above; Hermiticity, particle-hole symmetry and eigenvector residuals are checked separately. For open chains with \mu=t=\Delta=1 in common energy units, the smallest positive eigenvalues at lengths 8, 12 and 16 are approximately 0.00585989, 0.000366211 and 0.0000228882. The corresponding normalized eigenvectors place about 94% of their weight in the outermost two sites at each end. This demonstrates finite-size splitting and end localization for these parameters, not a universal protection scale.

A second independent check illustrates why zero energy is insufficient. At \mu=0 and t=\Delta=1, an eight-site open chain has two exact zero eigenvalues; the zero-subspace projector has one unit of Nambu weight at each end. A trivial chain at \mu=3 also acquires two zero eigenvalues if its first site is deliberately disconnected and tuned to zero on-site energy. Both projector weights then sit at that same site. The sum of two is a Nambu subspace dimension, not a measured charge. No leads or conductance are simulated here; this constructed counterexample tests the inference from energy alone.

For centrosymmetric, time-reversal-invariant, fully gapped odd-parity pairing, the Fu–Berg weak-pairing criterion supplies a useful sufficient test: the Fermi surface encloses an odd number of time-reversal-invariant momenta. In their three-dimensional setting the test detects the parity of an integer invariant. An even result does not establish that the integer itself vanishes. The normal-state Fermi-surface reduction assumes weak pairing and normal bands away from the chemical potential at those momenta. Do not apply it to an unspecified nodal, inversion-broken or time-reversal-broken state. 

 Experimental criteria

Distinguish intrinsic bulk order from an engineered interface. In the Fu–Kane proposal, ordinary s-wave proximity pairing gaps a topological-insulator surface. Its relation to a spinless p+ip description does not make the uniform surface a time-reversal-breaking chiral bulk superconductor: the uniform paired surface preserves time reversal, whereas a vortex changes the local setting. Surface participation in pairing and the actual defect or junction geometry matter. 

A zero-bias conductance peak alone does not uniquely identify a Majorana mode. Pan and Das Sarma construct alternatives involving quantum dots, spatially varying potentials and disorder. Their analysis also limits end-to-end correlation as a diagnostic: trivial correlations can occur, particularly in short wires, and accidental correlations require scrutiny even in longer examples. Length must be assessed relative to the relevant localization scales. Their model comparisons do not diagnose every experimental device. 

For an experimental claim, retain the full gate and field ranges, calibration, temperature, tunnel coupling and device-selection procedure. Compare local spectra with independent bulk-gap and nonlocal constraints. A measured gap reopening, a near-quantized peak or an isolated boundary feature must be assessed together with competing models; a checklist of individually ambiguous signatures cannot substitute for a state-specific argument.

A recent readout result illustrates a narrower, measurable advance. Van Loo and colleagues, published on 11 February 2026, report quantum-capacitance parity readout in a minimal two-site Kitaev chain, with switching lifetimes exceeding a millisecond and charge-sensing checks. Their abstract explicitly limits the protection of these minimal-chain modes relative to longer chains. Parity readout is not a demonstration of fault-tolerant braiding or a bulk material's superconducting transition. Here the published abstract and bibliographic record were checked; the full methods and raw data remain to be reviewed. 

 Limits and disputes

The 2018 claim titled “Quantized Majorana conductance” was retracted in 2021. The authors' retraction describes undisclosed charge-jump corrections, a mislabeled axis and recalibration that moved plateau values above the originally claimed quantized value. They withdrew the quantization claim. The original positive claim must not be reused as confirmation; the retraction does not by itself disprove every Majorana platform. 

Protection is conditional on the relevant gap, symmetries and isolation. Finite-size overlap, uncontrolled perturbations and changes of state need explicit treatment. The finite checks above establish neither a material invariant nor transport statistics, parity lifetime, fusion rules or a fault-tolerant operation. This entry does not promote a candidate compound to confirmed topological superconductivity. Full final-version comparisons and complete scientific acceptance remain open.

 Discovery implications

Start from a specified superconducting order and its dimensionality. Compute the appropriate invariant with convergence checks, predict boundary or defect responses in the actual geometry, and test alternatives against the same data range. Keep an engineered interface result separate from a host bulk-phase claim. Record negative results, corrections and the distinction between theoretical construction, compatible measurement and unique experimental identification.

 Related topics

Connect the paired-state description to , ,  and .

entries.title: Multiband and multichannel pairing
entries.summary: A coupling matrix determines a pairing instability. Multiple bands, interaction channels, transport channels and material phases are different concepts.

materialCases.sample: bulk magnesium diboride
materialCases.temperatureNote: approximate reported transition
materialCases.probe: discovery report; criterion not re-extracted in this review

materialCases.sample: single-layer interface
materialCases.temperatureNote: spectroscopic pairing scale, not assigned a transport Tc
materialCases.probe: ARPES and replica bands

entries.text:
Scope

Multiband pairing concerns how superconducting gaps on distinct bands are coupled. Multichannel pairing concerns different interaction contributions to a Cooper-pair kernel. Neither concept is equivalent to parallel normal-state electrical conductivities, and neither means that two spatially separate superconducting phases form one homogeneous condensate. Keeping these distinctions explicit prevents apparent evidence for several channels from becoming an unsupported mechanism claim.  

 Mathematical assumptions

For a simplified weak-coupling model with a shared cutoff energy Ec, a linearized gap equation can be written


\Deltai=L(Tc)\sumj\lambda{ij}\Deltaj,
\qquad
L(Tc)=\ln\!\left(\frac{1.13Ec}{kBTc}\right).


In this declared approximation, the largest relevant pairing eigenvalue sets the instability. Off-diagonal entries represent interband pair transfer and help constrain relative gap phases. A matrix eigenvalue is not the arithmetic sum of all its entries. The energy cutoff notation here makes the dimensions explicit when converting the original ASCII equation. 

The full problem can have different frequency spectra, momentum structure, repulsive terms, Coulomb effects and normal self-energy renormalization. Combining a pairing attraction and a mass enhancement into one positive scalar can give a misleading temperature estimate. Interactions can cooperate, compete or favor different gap structures after projection into the pairing channel. 

 Experimental criteria

Resolve gap magnitudes and their band assignments with complementary spectroscopy and thermodynamics. State the band or orbital basis, energy cutoff, Coulomb treatment and disorder model. Distinguish a measurement that observes two gaps from an inference that identifies two different mediating bosons. Normal-state two-component Drude fits do not by themselves establish two superconducting gaps.

The MgB2 discovery paper reports superconductivity near 39 K. The detailed sample and transition criterion have not been re-extracted in this review, so the material record keeps its criterion explicitly unknown. 

Choi and colleagues calculated band-dependent gaps in MgB2 using an anisotropic Eliashberg treatment of electron-phonon pairing. Their sigma- and pi-band gaps vanish at a common calculated transition temperature. This is a theoretical result consistent with multiple gaps within that model; it is not a direct measurement of two independent pairing mediators. 

 Material interpretation

In single-layer FeSe/SrTiO3, replica-band observations support the relevance of an interface electron-phonon interaction. They do not independently extract every spin, interface and plasmon contribution as a set of additive coupling constants. The interface hypothesis must be tested together with charge transfer, the reconstructed electronic structure and phase-coherence limitations. 

A high pairing or gap-closing scale measured by ARPES is not automatically a zero-resistance transition. When an interface and intrinsic electronic interactions are both discussed, the useful object is a specified combined kernel with assumptions and uncertainties. This pilot deliberately contains no unsourced table of separate FeSe/SrTiO3 coupling constants. 

 Limits and disputes

A common transition temperature is compatible with interband locking, but does not establish beneficial synergy between distinct interactions. Changes in a band structure, density of states or scattering rate can alter the instability without revealing a unique mediator. Cross-material percentages assigned to a plasmon enhancement are not universal physical constants.  

 Discovery implications

A testable multichannel proposal predicts a gap structure and its response to an independent control parameter. Show what would distinguish cooperation from competition, and check that the same interaction has not been counted twice. The most useful next measurement constrains a specific matrix element or spectral contribution rather than simply adding another possible mechanism to a list.

See , , and .

entries.title: Flat-band pairing
entries.summary: Separate pairing enhancement from phase coherence, and connect quantum geometry to measured total stiffness with the model and device conditions intact.

materialCases.sample: Tanaka earlier-author v2 representative microwave/DC device; not the Cao2018 device
materialCases.temperatureNote: 20 mK refrigerator base; approximately 40 mK wired device. Approximate half-resistance scale near 1 K across the dome is not assigned as one precise Tc.
materialCases.probe: Four-probe DC and microwave kinetic inductance; edge proximity and active-aspect-ratio model

entries.text:
Scope

A narrow band can increase the number of electronic states available for pairing, while reducing the ordinary velocity-based contribution to current response. Pair formation and phase coherence must therefore be assessed separately. A large density of states is not a guarantee of high superconducting transition temperature, and a flat band need not be topological.

Peotta and Törmä derive a geometric contribution to superfluid weight within a multiband mean-field treatment. Their isolated-flat-band reduction assumes bandwidth much smaller than attraction, attraction much smaller than the gaps to other bands, and a suitable uniform orbital pairing field. The associated Chern bound includes interaction, filling and normalization factors; it is not a dimensionful stiffness greater than a bare integer. Julku and colleagues give a Chern-trivial Lieb-lattice example with finite geometric response, so a nonzero Chern number is sufficient for particular bounds, not necessary for every geometric contribution.  

 Mathematical assumptions

Consider an independent reduced pairing model with one flat state per spin per cell, effective attraction G>0 and half filling. Absorb the Hartree shift into the chemical potential and set the flat level at that chemical potential. The mean-field equation is

1=\frac{G}{2\Delta}\tanh\!\left(\frac{\Delta}{2kBT}\right),\qquad \Delta(0)=\frac{G}{2},\qquad kBT{\mathrm{pair}}=\frac{G}{4}.

Twelve numerical cases solve the finite-temperature equation or verify the absence of a nonzero solution above its linearized onset. This linear pairing scale depends on the stated state-counting convention. It must not be transferred unchanged to a multiorbital lattice: the effective interaction includes orbital weights and differs from a bare on-site attraction.

To test whether pairing alone establishes coherence, take four disconnected attractive sites. Direct enumeration of all 256 occupation states at three attractions gives pair binding but no dependence of the spectrum or partition function on an intersite phase twist. The thermal trace of pair transfer between different sites is zero. Each site can bind two particles while the assembly carries no phase-stiffness response. The mean-field onset above is not a true finite-temperature superconducting transition in this atomic limit.

A second independent illustration keeps two exactly flat band energies but changes their eigenvectors in a fixed orbital basis. Compare a constant normalized vector with u(k)=(\cos(k/2),\sin(k/2)). The first has zero quantum metric; the second has

g{kk}=\langle\partialk u|\partialk u\rangle-|\langle u|\partialk u\rangle|^2=\frac14.

Twelve finite-difference fidelity checks reproduce these values, including a smooth momentum-dependent phase multiplying each vector. Identical dispersions therefore do not determine identical geometry. This Bloch-phase invariance does not remove the need to specify physical orbital positions, coupling to a field and the response of the pairing fields.

For the rotating vector, an imposed projected pair field has overlap |\langle u(k-q)|u(k+q)\rangle|^2=\cos^2q. With fixed \Delta and level offset \xi, define E(q)=\sqrt{\xi^2+\Delta^2\cos^2q} and the illustrative energy cost E(0)-E(q). Six finite-difference comparisons, including the constant-vector case, give curvature \Delta^2/E(0) for the rotating vector and zero for the constant one. If the pair phase gradient is Q=2q, its curvature is one quarter as large. This checks a frozen projected overlap response, not a self-consistent multiband stiffness or one-dimensional finite-temperature order.

For an isotropic superconducting sheet, define phase stiffness by F/A=\rhos|\nabla\theta-(2e/\hbar)\mathbf A|^2/2. Then sheet kinetic inductance L\square gives \rhos=\hbar^2/(4e^2L\square). A hypothetical zero-temperature value of 10 nH per square corresponds to \rhos/kB\approx0.784 K and an upper BKT scale of about 1.232 K. The actual BKT jump uses the renormalized stiffness just below the transition, not this zero-temperature value. This is a unit-conversion illustration, not a material measurement.

 Experimental criteria

Cao and colleagues established gate-tunable superconducting transport in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene. Their published device discussion uses four-probe measurements and deliberately non-superconducting Cr/Au contacts. These observations establish the platform, but do not uniquely separate phonon, electronic and geometric roles. Keep twist angle, density and transition criterion attached to the specific device rather than combining a maximum temperature from one device with a stiffness from another. 

Tanaka and colleagues infer total sheet stiffness from microwave kinetic inductance alongside four-probe transport. The reviewed earlier manuscript uses a 20 mK refrigerator base temperature and estimates about 40 mK for the wired device. Its circuit model includes a parallel electrode-proximitized edge, and the sheet conversion assumes the active region shares the device aspect ratio. The approximately 1 K scale across much of the dome uses half normal-state resistance; it is not automatically the zero-resistance or BKT temperature. Comparison with a conventional estimate supports a geometric interpretation without isolating a model-independent geometric fraction. These selected manuscript passages were checked; the complete published-version and raw-data comparison remains open. 

 Limits and disputes

The CsV3Sb5 discovery paper combines superconducting evidence with normal-state photoemission and band calculations. A kagome lattice, a van Hove feature, normal-state band topology and charge order are different observations. None alone measures quantum-metric superfluid weight or proves that geometry supplies the pairing interaction. Related potassium and rubidium compounds require their own specimen-specific review; no cross-compound temperature ranking is inferred here. 

A September 2026 preprint by Wang and colleagues studies a proposed pair-density-wave state with Bogoliubov Fermi surfaces. It predicts that residual zero-energy spectral weight can accompany reduced stiffness despite a positive geometric contribution. This is a model prediction, not an observed universal correlation. The current v2 title and abstract differ from the March v1 indexed by some services; this entry cites v2 explicitly and has checked only its abstract and version history. 

Neither the finite models above nor a fit to total stiffness identifies a unique pairing interaction. Orbital relaxation, remote bands, disorder and spatial inhomogeneity can alter quantitative comparisons. Full scientific acceptance remains open, including final-version checks, raw-data review and material-specific self-consistent response calculations.

 Discovery implications

Optimize pairing and coherence together. State the bandwidth, interband separation, orbital interaction and filling; test the approximations before applying an isolated-band formula. Compare gap, transport and inductive response in the same specimen. Keep an inferred phase scale separate from measured resistive criteria, and preserve the uncertainty in the conventional baseline used to discuss geometry.

 Related topics

Continue with , ,  and .

entries.title: Mottness and superconductivity
entries.summary: Distinguish localization, charge transfer and pairing, with spectral-weight checks and material-specific experimental conditions.
entries.text:
Scope

Mottness describes how electronic interactions constrain charge motion near integer filling and influence the states reached by doping or changing bandwidth. It is a useful starting point for some superconductors, not a unique pairing interaction. Anderson's RVB proposal is one historical route from a correlated parent; competing orders and several pairing descriptions remain part of the cuprate problem.  

Distinguish Mott-Hubbard and charge-transfer descriptions. In a localized configuration picture, the former emphasizes the cost of redistributing electrons between metal sites; the latter can involve a lower-energy ligand-to-metal excitation. Hybridization and bandwidth complicate that comparison. The Zaanen–Sawatzky–Allen paper provides the classification anchor, but its full text has not been checked here. The selected Lee–Nagaosa–Wen manuscript explicitly retains oxygen holes in cuprates before discussing a restricted low-energy reduction. A fitted single-band interaction is not automatically the bare metal-orbital Coulomb energy.  

 Mathematical assumptions

An independent Hubbard-dimer illustration separates charge and spin scales. Take two sites, two spin states per site, hopping t>0, repulsion U\geq0, and no ligand orbital or reservoir. With EN the lowest energy at fixed particle number, define the finite-system charge addition/removal gap \Deltac=E3+E1-2E2. Direct diagonalization gives

\Deltac=\sqrt{U^2+16t^2}-2t,\qquad \Deltas=\frac{\sqrt{U^2+16t^2}-U}{2}.

Here \Deltas is the two-electron singlet–triplet gap. Eight independent spectra verify these expressions and the total double occupancy obtained from \partial E2/\partial U. At U=0, the dimer already has a charge gap 2t from its discrete bonding levels. A finite-cluster charge gap therefore does not establish a bulk Mott transition. For U\gg t, the spin scale approaches 4t^2/U while the charge cost increases. Neither is a superconducting gap or a predicted transition temperature. The cited review supplies the Hubbard-model context; this calculation is an independent illustration. 

For a second atomic illustration, prescribe a spin-balanced ensemble with empty-site probability x, each singly occupied state of probability (1-x)/2, and no double occupancy. Counting electron creation and removal matrix elements gives, after summing both spins,

W{\mathrm{remove}}=1-x,\qquad W{\mathrm{add,low}}=2x,\qquad W{\mathrm{add,upper}}=1-x.

The total spectral weight is two; the lower-energy removal-plus-addition weight is 1+x, rather than a fixed rigid band with only its occupation changed. Five enumerated cases check the sum rule. This is a zero-hopping state-counting result with a specified ensemble, not a quantitative X-ray absorption spectrum. Finite hopping, ligand character and a core hole alter the interpretation of a measured spectrum.  

Configuration mixing also prevents an orbital label from being an integer occupancy. For the illustrative matrix H=\begin{pmatrix}0&V\\V&\Delta{\mathrm{CT}}\end{pmatrix} in two configuration states, the lower eigenstate has second-state weight [1-\Delta{\mathrm{CT}}/\sqrt{\Delta{\mathrm{CT}}^2+4V^2}]/2. Eight eigenvector and energy-derivative comparisons verify this result. The symbol \Delta{\mathrm{CT}} denotes a configuration-energy difference in this toy model; it is not a measured gap. This two-state calculation omits the lattice, multiplets and screening and cannot determine a material's ZSA phase boundary.  

 Experimental criteria

Chen and colleagues measured the oxygen K edge of La2-xSrxCuO4+δ using bulk-sensitive fluorescence yield. Their two pre-edge features evolve with Sr concentration; the reported modeling includes local interactions and core-hole excitonic correlations. This supports a doped charge-transfer interpretation without making absorption intensity a direct ground-state density of states or proving a pairing glue. The present check is abstract-scoped. 

Lefebvre and colleagues' kappa-Cl organic-salt study connects a pressure-driven Mott boundary with nearby antiferromagnetism and superconductivity. Its helium-pressure protocol includes 0.5 T NMR and AC susceptibility without a static field. Those are different measurement conditions, and the selected manuscript leaves macroscopic versus mesoscopic coexistence unresolved. No fixed pressure or transition temperature is transferred to other salts. 

Sun and colleagues' 2023 bilayer-nickelate report must retain sample and probe distinctions: four-probe resistance, KBr versus no pressure medium, nonzero residual resistance, and separately measured magnetic response. The published methods use room-temperature ruby calibration. Pressure changes structure as well as electronic parameters; the reported signatures do not identify Mottness as the pairing cause. 

 Limits and disputes

CeCu2Si2 supplies a heavy-fermion comparison, not a copy of a one-band copper-oxide model. Its original discovery supports superconductivity with strongly enhanced electronic response; that report does not settle a unique gap or pairing glue. Comparisons involving localized f states and itinerant coherence require a material-specific Kondo description. Effective mass alone is not a measurement of a Mott charge gap. 

Mottness is neither sufficient nor a universal prerequisite for superconductivity. MgB2 provides a multiband electron–phonon calculation, and sulfur-hydride experiments provide a distinct high-pressure setting. These examples prevent treating a doped Mott parent as a necessary route to a high transition scale. The inherited MgB2 DOI has been corrected to nature00898; the old nature00992 points to an unrelated biological channel paper.  

 Discovery implications

State the orbital basis, interaction convention and screening method before comparing U/t or charge-transfer energies. Combine transport with spectroscopic and structural measurements, preserving pressure media, oxygen content and temperature criteria. Treat localization, pseudogap, magnetic exchange, pairing and phase coherence as distinct questions. Full scientific acceptance, final-version comparisons and raw-data checks remain open; the finite models illustrate constraints rather than rank real materials.   

 Related topics

Read , , , , and .

entries.title: Migdal–Eliashberg theory: retardation and strong-coupling limits
entries.summary: Connect spectral functions, frequency-dependent pairing and Coulomb cutoffs. Distinguish numerical convergence, approximation validity and experimental evidence.
entries.text:
Scope

Migdal–Eliashberg theory describes a frequency-dependent electronic self-energy and pairing response to a retarded interaction. The renormalization function Z and anomalous self-energy \phi define \Delta=\phi/Z. A phonon-mediated calculation needs an electronic structure, phonon spectrum and interaction model; a large fitted coupling is not by itself evidence for a microscopic mechanism.

Migdal's original paper treats a normal metal and explicitly says that extension to the superconducting state requires a separate investigation. Its selected vertex discussion uses a separation of electronic and lattice scales with specified momentum regimes. The inherited DOI points to an unrelated primatology article; the correct historical JETP scan is retained without inventing a DOI. 

 Mathematical assumptions

Use phonon energy \Omega and Matsubara energies \omegan=(2n+1)\pi kBT; factors of \hbar are absorbed when converting angular frequencies to energies. For the isotropic spectral function a(\Omega)=\alpha^2F(\Omega), define

\lambda=2\int0^\infty\frac{a(\Omega)}{\Omega}\,d\Omega,\qquad K(\nu)=2\int0^\infty\frac{\Omega a(\Omega)}{\Omega^2+\nu^2}\,d\Omega.

Thus K(0)=\lambda. Neither this spectral coupling nor a band-resolved coupling matrix is an arbitrary pairing eigenvalue. The selected review derives the imaginary-axis equations under stated electronic-density-of-states and symmetry approximations. 

An independent positive-mode example writes a(\Omega)=\sumi\lambdai\Omegai\delta(\Omega-\Omegai)/2. It gives \lambda=\sumi\lambdai and K(\nu)=\sumi\lambdai\Omegai^2/(\Omegai^2+\nu^2). With normalized weights wi=\lambdai/\lambda, the logarithmic energy is \Omega{\log}=\Omega{\rm ref}\exp[\sumiwi\ln(\Omegai/\Omega{\rm ref})]; the arbitrary positive reference cancels. The second moment is \langle\Omega^2\rangle=\sumiwi\Omegai^2.

One mode with \lambda=1 at energy \Omega0 and two modes with couplings 1/2 at \Omega0/2 and 2\Omega0 have the same \lambda and \Omega{\log}. Their root-mean-square energies differ by a factor \sqrt{17/8}, and at \nu=\Omega0/2 their kernels are 0.8 and approximately 0.72059. This independently checked counterexample shows why two scalar summaries do not specify the full spectral problem.

For an isotropic, particle-hole-symmetric constant-density-of-states model with a fixed phonon kernel and zero Coulomb term, the linearized gap equation is

Zn\Deltan=\pi kBT\summ K(\omegan-\omegam)\frac{\Deltam}{|\omegam|}.

The sum covers positive and negative fermion frequencies. The normal-state Zn must be calculated from the same kernel; omitting it changes the theory. We solve the equivalent symmetric positive-frequency eigenproblem, locating the temperature where its largest eigenvalue reaches one. Increasing the retained positive frequencies from 16 to 128 gives kBTc/\Omega0\simeq0.11462 for a single mode with \lambda=1. For a 10 meV mode this is about 13.30 K, consistent with the review's model benchmark. It is not an experimental transition or a prediction for a named material. 

A scalar logarithmic Coulomb reduction has the conditional form \mu^=\mu/[1+\mu\ln(E{\rm el}/Ec)]. It assumes well-separated cutoffs and the stated constant-density-of-states treatment. Reducing the energy range in two successive steps gives the same result as one step; independently checked differentiation gives d\mu^/d\ln(E{\rm el}/Ec)=-(\mu^)^2. Report the cutoff with the number: changing the cutoff while keeping \mu^ fixed changes the model. Morel–Anderson's original abstract and the later review are distinct evidence scopes.  

 Experimental criteria

Choi and colleagues' MgB2 work uses anisotropic first-principles Eliashberg calculations to connect band-dependent gaps with a common calculated transition. These are theoretical results. The corrected DOI is nature00898, not the inherited unrelated nature00992. Agreement with observations must be assessed with sample and computational conditions preserved. 

Drozdov and colleagues' sulfur-hydride author abstract reports resistive, magnetic-field and susceptibility evidence, with an isotope comparison. It attributes the high-temperature phase to likely H3S formed from pressurized H2S. This entry retains that version-specific attribution and does not claim a new structural identification or independent reanalysis. 

The cited lanthanum-superhydride paper is by Somayazulu and colleagues, not Drozdov. Its publisher abstract describes four-probe transport drops at 180–200 GPa and supporting characterization. Do not combine its sample, pressure or criterion with a different LaH10 report merely because both discuss lanthanum hydrides. No sample-specific transition value is extracted here. 

For a material calculation, preserve the crystal phase, pressure, stability analysis, electronic and phonon meshes, spectral normalization, Coulomb treatment and convergence. Distinguish harmonic from anharmonic phonons and isotropic from anisotropic or multiband kernels. An inverted tunneling spectrum is model-dependent evidence, not a direct measurement of the interaction function.

 Limits and disputes

McMillan and Allen–Dynes expressions summarize particular Eliashberg solutions; they are not universal bounds. The Allen–Dynes abstract explicitly identifies errors at large coupling and correction factors depending on spectral shape. A fixed-spectrum strong-coupling asymptote does not prove that a real crystal remains stable while its coupling increases without limit. Their full original derivations and datasets are outside this scoped check.  

A small phonon-to-electron energy ratio alone does not certify every approximation. Narrow bands, unusual momentum structure, phonon feedback and polaron physics require specific analysis. Chubukov and colleagues' abstract compares a model's Migdal results with quantum Monte Carlo and identifies a breakdown of some normal-state properties. This is a model result, not a universal numerical coupling threshold for all materials. 

Real-axis spectra require analytic continuation and its numerical checks. An imaginary-axis gap value is not automatically a measured spectral edge; finite damping and multiple bands complicate that correspondence. Replacing the phonon kernel with a spin or charge fluctuation interaction requires a new justification of the approximation and evidence chain.

 Discovery implications

Use spectral calculations to test a candidate mechanism against consistent thermodynamic, spectroscopic and structural evidence. Compare sensitivity to the Coulomb term and phonon treatment rather than selecting whichever inputs yield the largest transition temperature. Keep numerical convergence, validity of the physical approximation and agreement with experiment as three separate judgments.

entries.title: Antiferromagnetic spin fluctuations: pairing and evidence
entries.summary: How repulsive interactions can favor sign-changing gaps, why magnetic signals do not prove a mechanism, and how probe limits and published corrections constrain the evidence.
entries.text:
Scope

Antiferromagnetic spin fluctuations are a candidate pairing interaction with substantial weight at a nonzero momentum transfer. A repulsive interaction can favor a gap that changes sign between the states it connects. This is a model-dependent mechanism proposal: observing magnetism, or finding superconductivity near an antiferromagnetic phase, does not establish causation. 

Keep three questions separate: are magnetic fluctuations present; do they change systematically with superconductivity; and can a consistently specified interaction reproduce pairing and other observables? An affirmative answer to the first two does not by itself answer the third. The relevant Fermi surfaces, orbitals, frequency dependence and competing channels must be specified.

 Mathematical assumptions

A dressed particle-particle eigenproblem can be written, with kB=1 and k including momentum and Matsubara frequency, as

-\frac{T}{N}\sum{k'}\Gamma^{pp}(k,k')G\uparrow(k')G\downarrow(-k')\phi(k')=\Lambda(T)\phi(k).

Here N is the number of lattice sites and the Green functions and irreducible pairing vertex must belong to the same approximation. A leading eigenvalue reaching one signals a pairing instability within that treatment; it is not a measurement of a material transition. The selected review gives this equation and distinguishes spin, charge and fully irreducible contributions. 

An independently checked static illustration uses two patches with positive single-spin density-of-states weights Nh,Ne, a common pairing cutoff, constant gaps and repulsive interactions Uh,Ue,V. After the common energy logarithm is factored out, define \eta\Deltai=-\sumjV{ij}Nj\Deltaj. The rescaling xi=\sqrt{Ni}\Deltai gives a symmetric matrix with diagonal elements -UiNi and off-diagonal element -V\sqrt{NhNe}.

Its larger eigenvalue is

\eta+=-\frac{UhNh+UeNe}{2}+\sqrt{\frac{(UhNh-UeNe)^2}{4}+V^2NhNe}.

For nonnegative intrapatch repulsions it is positive precisely when V^2>UhUe. If both Ui vanish, \eta+=V\sqrt{NhNe} and \Deltah/\Deltae=-\sqrt{Ne/Nh}. Five numerical checks verify the original and symmetrized equations, including unequal weights and the zero-eigenvalue boundary. These are illustrative pairing strengths, not the phonon spectral coupling \lambda, a calculated transition temperature, or a fit to any material.

A second independent check shows why a wavevector alone cannot select the gap symmetry. With lattice spacing one, both \cos kx-\cos ky and \cos kx+\cos ky reverse sign under \mathbf Q=(\pi,\pi). Under a ninety-degree rotation the former changes sign while the latter does not. Their values on the actual Fermi surface and their interaction-weighted eigenvalues still differ. A sign-reversal condition is therefore insufficient to select a unique representation.

 Experimental criteria

Neutron, RIXS and NMR measurements have different response functions, selection rules and energy windows. In the magnetic low-frequency limit, NMR relaxation has the schematic dependence 1/(T1T)\propto\sum{\mathbf q,\alpha\perp H}|A\alpha(\mathbf q)|^2\lim{\omega\to0}\chi''\alpha(\mathbf q,\omega)/\omega. The hyperfine weights and perpendicular spin components matter. The cited spin-chain paper supplies the response formula; it does not make that chain a superconducting-material example. NMR is not a momentum-resolved magnetic spectrum. 

RIXS intensities also require a scattering model. Ament and colleagues' indirect-RIXS treatment contains charge and spin response contributions whose relative weights depend on incident energy and the stated core-hole approximation. A measured peak should not automatically be identified with the pairing kernel. This abstract-scoped example is not a derivation for every direct-RIXS geometry. 

A superconducting spin resonance can reflect feedback of a sign-changing gap through coherence factors. Its interpretation still needs the normal-state response and a susceptibility calculation; it is not independent proof that the resonance caused pairing. 

The Tsuei–Kirtley review describes phase-sensitive evidence for predominantly d-wave pairing in specified optimally doped cuprates. Such symmetry evidence constrains mechanisms without uniquely identifying their microscopic origin. No sample-specific temperature or raw-data reanalysis is added here. 

 Limits and disputes

Mazin and colleagues proposed a compound-specific sign-changing extended-s state for fluorine-doped LaFeAsO. Their published note 8 revises the initial identification of the magnetic instability involved in the doping argument. Reading only the abstract can miss that qualification. Kuroki and colleagues' five-orbital RPA study likewise has parameter-dependent s- and d-wave competition. Neither result assigns one state to every iron-based material.  

Kuroki's 2009 erratum corrects an orbital-to-band transformation error affecting the original gap plot. For the displayed parameter set, the corrected diagonal band gap is fully open on the Fermi surface. The authors retain strong anisotropy and parameter-dependent nodal or competing d-wave possibilities. Cite the original together with the erratum; the original nodal plot is not the corrected result. This check reads the erratum text, not a reproduction of its band calculation.  

Monthoux–Pines report strong-coupling calculations for a YBCO model, including sensitivity to the spin spectrum and impurity treatment. Their calculated temperature is a theoretical result under chosen parameters. Agreement with selected data is a test of that model, not a mechanism proof that can be transferred to unrelated samples. 

A kernel validated for one cuprate must not be transferred unchanged to iron-based compounds or nickelates. Band occupation, orbital weights, interlayer coupling and pressure or strain can alter the relevant low-energy problem. Nickelate material records remain separate; this entry makes no new nickelate gap assignment. Compare normal self-energy, gap structure, magnetic response and competing channels using compatible parameters.

 Discovery implications

Record the measured composition, phase and conditions; spectral normalization and coverage; electronic structure; and the approximation linking response to pairing. Compare alternative channels and report the prediction that could discriminate them. Numerical convergence, agreement with one observable and uniqueness of a mechanism are separate checks. This article's finite-model calculations establish algebraic consistency only.

entries.title: Ferromagnetic fluctuations and odd-parity pairing
entries.summary: Separate triplet-pairing models from magnetic evidence, compare uranium compounds under stated conditions, and trace the limits of Knight shifts and critical fields.

materialCases.sample: Zambra et al.2026 single-crystal magnetotropic response
materialCases.temperatureNote: 4 K normal-state measurement;300mK superconducting boundaries in comparison figure are from earlier work
materialCases.probe: Pulsed fields up to60T; field rotations in ac/bc planes; transverse susceptibility inferred from magnetotropic response

entries.text:
Scope

Ferromagnetic fluctuations describe enhanced magnetic response near zero momentum transfer. They can support odd-parity pairing in specified models, but neither a large uniform susceptibility nor a large upper critical field identifies a superconducting spin state. Magnetic order, correlations, gap symmetry and the pairing interaction are separate questions. Fay and Appel calculated equal-spin p-state pairing from longitudinal fluctuations in an itinerant-electron model; this is a theoretical possibility, not a universal material classification. 

 Mathematical assumptions

For a simple effective exchange V=-J\boldsymbol{\sigma}1\cdot\boldsymbol{\sigma}2 with J>0, the spin operator has eigenvalues -3 in the singlet and +1 in the triplet sector. The corresponding interaction eigenvalues are +3J and -J. This independent two-spin illustration assumes a ferromagnetic effective interaction; it does not derive a material's exchange constant or its frequency dependence.

For even-frequency, single-orbital pairing, Fermi antisymmetry requires \Delta(\mathbf k)=-\Delta^T(-\mathbf k). Writing a triplet matrix as \Delta=(\mathbf d\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma)i\sigmay gives a symmetric spin matrix, so \mathbf d(-\mathbf k)=-\mathbf d(\mathbf k). Odd parity here follows from these assumptions. Strong spin–orbit coupling requires a suitable pseudospin description; additional orbital or frequency structure changes this elementary argument.

A second independent illustration uses a circular two-dimensional Fermi surface and an attractive angular kernel V(\theta)=-g/(a-b\cos\theta), with g>0 an energy scale and dimensionless a>b>0. Its dimensionless Fourier coefficients are

C\ell=\int0^{2\pi}\frac{d\theta}{2\pi}\frac{\cos(\ell\theta)}{a-b\cos\theta}=\frac{r^\ell}{\sqrt{a^2-b^2}},\qquad r=\frac{a-\sqrt{a^2-b^2}}{b},\quad \ell\geq0.

The odd-parity projection [V(\theta)-V(\theta+\pi)]/2 retains odd angular harmonics. Since 0<r<1, the strongest attractive odd harmonic in this example is \ell=1. Numerical quadrature checks the coefficients and projection. Crystal anisotropy, competing interactions and self-energy are absent: this example neither selects a universal p-wave state nor predicts a transition temperature.

 Experimental criteria

UGe2 superconductivity was reported in a restricted pressure range within an itinerant-ferromagnetic setting. URhGe supplied ambient-pressure thermodynamic evidence for coexistence; UCoGe supplied ambient-pressure superconducting and ferromagnetic signatures. These primary abstracts support the historical observations, while microscopic volume overlap and a particular gap representation require more than proximity in a phase diagram. Corrected original links replace two inherited citation errors.   

Lévy and colleagues reported a second superconducting pocket in URhGe around spin-axis reorientation near 12 T for field parallel to the crystal b axis, after low-field superconductivity had already disappeared. This is an orientation-specific re-entrant phenomenon. The original abstract suggests a connection to spin rotation; it does not uniquely establish a microscopic pairing kernel. 

Pustogow and colleagues' 2019 Sr2RuO4 author manuscript reports a reduced oxygen-17 Knight shift and strong pulse-energy sensitivity. Its unstrained example uses an in-plane b-axis field of 0.7107 T; 20 mK is the base temperature, not a transition temperature. Selected methods explain why RF heating and different electronic/nuclear relaxation times can make a relaxation check insufficient. These observations challenge older unchanged-susceptibility interpretations; this entry does not infer a unique order parameter from them. 

UTe2's discovery paper reported unusual anisotropic critical fields in a paramagnetic normal state. Its page 2 distinguishes a highest measured field of 20 T from an estimated zero-temperature b-axis value of 40 T. The estimate is not a measured endpoint. Historical triplet and ferromagnetic-pairing interpretations remain interpretations; the paper's schematic does not establish one continuous phase diagram shared by different uranium compounds. 

Record field direction, pressure, composition, purity and temperature for each probe. Separate orbital/background contributions and pulse heating in Knight shifts; retain coupling, g-factor, multiband and orbital-limiting assumptions in critical-field comparisons. Combine symmetry-sensitive measurements with magnetic and superconducting volume evidence from the same sample. A bulk signal alone does not identify the mediating fluctuation.

 Limits and disputes

In UTe2, Duan and colleagues reported a neutron resonance associated with antiferromagnetic wavevectors. Their extended-data comparison found no ferromagnetic signal above background in the stated measurement window. This is not absence of every possible small-momentum fluctuation at every field, energy and temperature; a resonance coupled to superconductivity also does not alone prove the direction of causation. 

A study published on 29 April 2026 measured UTe2 magnetotropic response in pulsed fields up to 60 T at 4 K, where the studied superconducting phases were suppressed. It inferred enhanced transverse, near-zero-momentum susceptibility at high fields. Here transverse means perpendicular to the applied field, not an off-diagonal tensor component. These normal-state measurements differ from zero/low-field neutron conditions. The displayed 300 mK superconducting boundaries came from earlier work, and 4 K must not be recorded as this experiment's superconducting transition. 

Fluctuations can enhance attraction while also renormalizing quasiparticles and affecting pair breaking. Fay–Appel's model gives a maximum followed by a decrease of calculated transition temperature toward the magnetic transition. Neither that model nor the elementary angular projection proves a universal optimum at a ferromagnetic quantum critical point. Longitudinal/transverse spectral weight, spin–orbit coupling and band structure must be specified. 

 Discovery implications

Treat small-momentum magnetic response as a candidate-screening observation. Test whether a proposed kernel simultaneously explains symmetry constraints, normal-state responses and field/pressure trends under matched conditions. Keep negative observations and alternative channels. The recent UTe2 comparison illustrates why distinct experiments should retain their conditions instead of being reduced to a single ferromagnetic or antiferromagnetic label. Selected source passages and model checks here leave full scientific acceptance open.

 Related topics

Compare ,  and the keyword catalogue for gap symmetry, critical fields and uranium material families.

entries.title: Nematic fluctuations: pairing enhancement and evidence
entries.summary: Connect symmetry-sensitive response with candidate pairing models while separating strain from stress, nematic form factors from gaps, and correlation from causation.
entries.text:
Scope

Electronic nematic order breaks a crystal's rotational symmetry without requiring a new translation period. This entry concerns the associated fluctuations as a candidate pairing interaction; observing static anisotropy is a different question. Spin, orbital and lattice responses can couple, so the name of a measured response does not identify its microscopic origin. The Fernandes–Chubukov–Schmalian review provides background on that distinction. 

Lederer and colleagues study a weakly coupled metal near an Ising nematic quantum critical point. Their controlled regime excludes a narrow region closest to criticality. Nematic fluctuations can enhance several pairing channels, with the background interaction often selecting the leading symmetry. This conditional result is not a universal transition-temperature law for iron compounds, cuprates or nickelates. 

 Mathematical assumptions

A transparent static illustration uses dimensionless electronic order \phi and symmetry-matched strain \epsilon. Let the quadratic free-energy density be

F=\frac{r}{2}\phi^2+\frac{C}{2}\epsilon^2-g\phi\epsilon-h\phi-s\epsilon.

Here h is a source conjugate to electronic order and s is the corresponding stress. With this normalization, r,C,g,h,s have units of energy density. The symmetric phase is locally stable when r>0, C>0 and rC>g^2. This is a uniform, equilibrium, small-response model; it omits spatial dynamics, domains and critical fluctuations. It makes the boundary-condition distinction in the Chu manuscript explicit. 

At fixed strain, \partial\phi/\partial h=1/r and \partial\phi/\partial\epsilon=g/r. Allowing strain to relax at fixed stress instead gives

\left.\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial h}\right|s=\frac{C}{rC-g^2},\qquad\left.\frac{\partial\phi}{\partial s}\right|h=\frac{g}{rC-g^2},\qquad C{\mathrm{eff}}=C-\frac{g^2}{r}.

These derivatives are not interchangeable susceptibilities. Independent minimization checks all four parameter examples. A measured resistance anisotropy can have a linear proxy form N=c\phi+b\epsilon, giving dN/d\epsilon=cg/r+b in the clamped electronic-response model. Conversion to electronic susceptibility therefore needs a proxy coefficient and background assumptions, not just the observation of a large resistance slope.

Adding a stabilizing u\phi^4/4 term changes the strain response about a finite biased state to g/(r+3u\phi0^2) for u>0. Three independent nonlinear-solution checks recover this derivative. Residual strain can round a response; this illustration does not calibrate a piezo stack or determine a material's critical temperature.

For the pairing problem, the nematic form factor is not the gap function. In Lederer's model, the induced vertex contains the squared magnitude of a nematic form factor and a susceptibility concentrated near zero momentum transfer. Its sign, normalization and frequency window belong to that model. Selected published equations and the author manuscript were checked; the full microscopic calculation was not reproduced. 

An independent circular-Fermi-surface illustration takes f(\theta)=\cos2\theta and a positive forward-limit correction \delta\lambda=\eta\langle f^2|\Delta|^2\rangle, with dimensionless \eta>0 and normalized trial functions. For \Delta=1,\sqrt2\cos2\theta,\sqrt2\sin2\theta,\sqrt2\cos\theta, direct quadrature gives overlaps 1/2,3/4,1/4,1/2. Several channels are enhanced by the same nematic form factor. These illustrative overlaps exclude finite-width mixing, self-energy and lattice anisotropy; they neither establish the winning material gap nor yield an experimental transition temperature.

 Experimental criteria

Chu and colleagues measured strain-induced resistance changes in Co-substituted BaFe2As2. Selected author-manuscript methods distinguish controlled strain from controlled stress and check strain transmission. A PubMed record flags a later correction; its publisher text remains unavailable in this review, so final-version reconciliation stays open. No numerical phase boundary is extracted here.  

Kuo and colleagues' earlier manuscript studies differential elastoresistance in five optimally doped iron-based families, including FeTeSe. P-substituted BaFe2As2 follows Curie–Weiss behavior over a wider measured temperature interval; several other samples deviate at lower temperature. Thus the cited study already contains chalcogenide evidence, but it does not establish universal behavior across every composition. Its B2g label uses stated tetragonal axes; rotating axis conventions changes symmetry labels. Exact composition reconciliation with the final paper remains pending. 

Romero and colleagues' earlier manuscript measures complex THz conductivity of FeTeSe films and fits parallel conduction channels. It discusses a qualitative resemblance to nematic-fluctuation models. Conductivity and a successful channel fit are not direct measurements of the Cooper-pairing vertex; the manuscript-to-final-article comparison remains incomplete. 

For each experiment retain the strain component, coordinate system, stress or strain boundary condition, transmission calibration, thermal-contraction offset and linear-response window. Separate symmetry-breaking response from isotropic background. Compare elastoresistance, Raman and elastic measurements only after stating their frequency, momentum, lattice-coupling and proxy assumptions. Matching trends do not make different response functions identical.

 Limits and disputes

A Curie–Weiss extrapolation defines a model-dependent temperature scale. It need not be the measured structural transition, and neither is automatically the superconducting transition. Disorder, finite bias, competing magnetism and changing transport coefficients can affect the inference. The static illustrative free energy above contains no dynamical pairing kernel and therefore cannot prove that the measured fluctuations cause superconductivity.

A small-momentum interaction can be an amplifier without uniquely fixing gap sign. Near degeneracy, even a modest channel-dependent correction can change the leading state; away from degeneracy, background interactions may keep their ordering. Strong critical feedback can invalidate the controlled approximation. A complete comparison must include the normal self-energy as well as the anomalous pairing interaction.

 Discovery implications

Use a candidate nematic response to design matched symmetry-resolved measurements and competing-channel calculations. Ask whether one model explains gap anisotropy, normal-state response and tuning trends on comparable samples. Nickelates remain an open target for such tests; an iron-based mechanism cannot simply be assigned to them. Preserve evidence against the hypothesis alongside supporting correlations, and distinguish a scoped source check from full scientific acceptance.

 Related topics

Compare , ,  and the keyword catalogue for strain and gap-symmetry entries.

entries.title: Charge fluctuations, CDW proximity and pairing
entries.summary: Separate static competition, coexistence and candidate charge-assisted pairing; distinguish charge density waves from modulated pair fields.
entries.text:
Scope

Charge fluctuations at finite wave vector are a candidate contribution to a superconducting pairing interaction. Three observations must stay distinct: a static charge density wave (CDW) can compete with superconductivity; two orders can coexist; and dynamic charge fluctuations can contribute to pairing in a specified model. Neither coexistence nor a nearby superconducting dome alone establishes the third claim.

Castellani, Di Castro and Grilli studied quasiparticle scattering near charge instabilities in an infinite-U Hubbard–Holstein model. Their abstract distinguishes a zero-momentum singularity without long-range Coulomb forces from a finite-momentum singularity when those forces are included. This model context does not turn bare Coulomb repulsion into universal attraction. Only its publisher abstract was checked here; the original calculation has not been reproduced. 

 Mathematical assumptions

An independent Gaussian illustration makes one sign convention explicit. For a real normalized mode \phi, density source n, positive static susceptibility \chi and real coupling g, take an energy F=\phi^2/(2\chi)+gn\phi. Completing the square, or integrating the Gaussian, gives

F{\mathrm{eff}}(n)-F{\mathrm{eff}}(0)=-\frac{g^2\chi}{2}n^2.

With dimensionless \phi,n, g has energy units and \chi inverse-energy units. Three numerical integrals independently recover this shift in normalized units. This result concerns an already specified bosonic mode. A real material requires screened vertices, momentum and frequency dependence, and any residual Coulomb terms; double counting the same charge response as two separate interactions is not justified.

A two-patch illustration absorbs density-of-states weights into dimensionless interactions u within each patch and v between patches. For equal weights, the linearized pairing matrix is K=-\begin{pmatrix}u&v\\v&u\end{pmatrix}. The equal-sign and opposite-sign eigenvalues are -u-v and -u+v. Attractive interpatch v<0 favors equal signs in this simplified space; repulsive v>0 favors opposite signs. Four independent Rayleigh-quotient searches verify the ordering, including a case where neither eigenvalue is positive. Finite-Q scattering alone therefore does not fix a gap symmetry. Frequency cutoffs, self-energy and a full Fermi surface are absent here.

Static competition is another problem. Let x=|\Delta|^2 and y=|\rho|^2 be nonnegative, dimensionless squared superconducting and CDW amplitudes, with

F=asx+\frac{bs}{2}x^2+acy+\frac{bc}{2}y^2+\gamma xy.

All coefficients have energy-density units. Assume bs,bc>0 and \gamma>-\sqrt{bsbc} so the quartic form is bounded on the physical quadrant. A stable interior mixed minimum additionally needs bsbc-\gamma^2>0 and positive solutions of the two stationarity equations. Otherwise boundary minima must be compared. Positive \gamma penalizes simultaneous amplitudes but can still allow coexistence. Four independent grid minimizations check mixed and boundary cases. This equilibrium model neither supplies a retarded pairing interaction nor predicts a material transition temperature.

 Experimental criteria

Ghiringhelli and colleagues used resonant soft x-ray scattering on underdoped Y/Nd barium cuprates. Selected manuscript passages resolve a near-zero-loss charge feature from larger-loss excitations and separate planar from chain contributions. The reported instrumental energy resolution is approximately 130 meV; the authors infer an upper energy bound of 20 meV for the CDW contribution. That bound is not a resolved pairing-boson peak. Increasing charge correlations toward the superconducting transition and their subsequent weakening support competition within the measured samples. 

Chang and colleagues studied a detwinned YBa2Cu3O6.67 crystal with 100 keV x-rays and fields up to 17 T. Its stated superconducting transition is 67 K, while charge modulation appears around 135 K. The selected manuscript reports charge order already at zero field; field enhancement below the superconducting transition accompanies suppression of superconductivity. Those two temperatures describe different phenomena, and diffraction intensity alone does not measure the Cooper-pairing vertex. 

For a pairing-mechanism claim, require the dynamic response over a stated momentum/energy window, the electron–mode vertex and screening convention, and a calculation that tests competing channels. Compare the same model against normal self-energy, gap structure and transition behavior on matched samples. Background subtraction, energy resolution, disorder, field orientation and tuning protocol must remain attached to experimental claims.

 Limits and disputes

Kusmartseva and colleagues report pressure-induced superconductivity in pristine 1T-TiSe2. Their abstract describes a superconducting region between approximately 2 and 4 GPa and cautions that pressure and copper intercalation can produce different electronic states. The full measurement protocol is not audited here, so this entry does not create a sample-specific transition record. A dome near CDW suppression is evidence of a relationship to investigate, not a unique mechanism assignment. 

Ortiz and colleagues' CsV3Sb5 discovery paper is Physical Review Letters 125, 247002. Its abstract combines bulk superconductivity with normal-state topological-band evidence and a higher-temperature CDW-like instability. This does not establish topological superconductivity, a particular gap sign or charge-mediated pairing. The inherited citation to Physical Review Materials 4, 121801 actually identifies an Osada praseodymium-nickelate paper; the public bibliography is corrected while the original source file is preserved. 

A pair density wave (PDW) modulates a pair field rather than simply the charge density. For coherent components \Delta+e^{iQx}+\Delta-e^{-iQx}, the 2Q Fourier coefficient of the squared amplitude is \Delta+\Delta-^. Three direct Fourier checks include the single-component counterexample, where that coefficient vanishes. Berg and colleagues describe a symmetry-allowed coupling \rho{-2Q}\Delta-^\Delta++\mathrm{c.c.}; its coefficient can vanish at exact particle–hole symmetry. Charge order alone does not imply PDW order. Pair-sensitive measurements and phase/alternative-signal controls remain necessary. 

 Discovery implications

Use CDW proximity to select competing hypotheses and measurements, not to label a mechanism prematurely. Require independent CDW evidence before including PdTe2 or beta-Bi2Pd as charge-mediated candidates. Likewise, a high-temperature resistive onset in a pressure-quenched cuprate cannot establish CDW causation without additional measurements. Keep lattice, spin, charge and multiband explanations available until their quantitative predictions are tested. The calculations above illustrate inference limits; the remaining final-version, raw-data and full scientific audits stay open.

 Related topics

Compare , ,  and the keyword catalogue for charge order and pair density waves.

entries.title: Exciton-mediated pairing: proposals and evidence boundaries
entries.summary: Distinguish electronic-excitation pairing proposals from neutral exciton condensation and transient optical signatures, with screening and model disputes explicit.

materialCases.sample: Budden author manuscript Fig4 photoexcited pellet
materialCases.temperatureNote: Base temperature of driven response; not equilibrium Tc
materialCases.probe: 1ns two-terminal voltage probe; contacts calibrated by static four-terminal measurements; about25mJ/cm2 pump fluence and75ps transport pump duration

entries.text:
Scope

Exciton-mediated superconductivity proposes that electronic excitations help bind charged Cooper pairs. It is distinct from condensation of neutral electron–hole pairs and from enhanced pair correlations in a driven finite cluster. This article does not designate a verified material realization of the mechanism; that editorial boundary is not a claim that an exhaustive worldwide search has excluded one.

Little's organic-polymer proposal and the Allender–Bray–Bardeen metal–semiconductor model are historical theoretical starting points. The latter considers metal electrons tunneling into a semiconductor and coupling to virtual excitons, with interface overlap and screening essential. Their high calculated transition scales are predictions under model assumptions, not measured material records. The original publisher abstracts were checked; the full calculations remain unaudited here.  

 Mathematical assumptions

A higher boson energy does not automatically raise a transition scale. An independent weak-coupling illustration assumes an electronic cutoff E, mode energy \Omega\lt E, attraction \lambda, and repulsion \mu, all couplings dimensionless:

\mu^=\frac{\mu}{1+\mu\ln(E/\Omega)},\qquad kBT{\mathrm{model}}=1.13\Omega\exp\left[-\frac{1}{\lambda-\mu^}\right].

This illustration requires \lambda>\mu^ and separated electronic and bosonic scales; it omits self-energy, momentum structure and interface geometry. It is not a reproduction of the historical exciton model. At fixed E,\lambda,\mu, differentiation gives

\frac{d\ln T{\mathrm{model}}}{d\ln\Omega}=1-\frac{(\mu^)^2}{(\lambda-\mu^)^2}.

Five finite-difference checks and an independent cutoff scan show that the prefactor gain can lose to reduced retardation of repulsion. The illustrative optimum for E=1000, \lambda=0.30, \mu=0.25 is \Omega\simeq69.5 in the same arbitrary energy unit. None of these numbers is a measured temperature. As \Omega/E increases, the assumed scale separation itself becomes less credible; this formula cannot certify electronic-boson superconductivity.

For a separate symmetry illustration, take three isolated states with energies 0,3,2 and inversion parities even, odd, even. An odd dipole operator connects the intermediate state to the other two, but has no direct matrix element between them. A drive F\cos t can therefore access the final even state through two interactions. Direct time evolution, with halved time steps and conserved norm, gives a final-state probability ratio of about 15.98 when a sufficiently weak field doubles, consistent with the perturbative F^4 limit. At larger fields the ratio is about 15.61: the power law is an asymptote. This isolated three-state check contains neither a condensate nor a relaxation bath.

Neutral interlayer coherence can be represented by \langle c1^\dagger c2\rangle. It is invariant under a common electronic phase rotation, unlike a charged Cooper-pair amplitude. An ideal relative-phase response has a normalized stiffness matrix proportional to \begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix}: the common layer-field direction has zero eigenvalue, while the difference direction has finite stiffness. Three direct response checks produce equal and opposite layer currents. This illustration excludes tunneling, contacts and additional charged channels; it does not predict an entire device's electromagnetic response.

 Experimental criteria

A convincing exciton-pairing attribution needs an independently characterized electronic mode, a screened coupling calculation and a controlled change of that mode that tracks pairing observables. Establish superconductivity separately through suitable transport and magnetic evidence. Then compare phonon, spin, plasmon, structural and interface alternatives on the same samples. A spectral peak, optical resonance or conductive interface alone does not select the mechanism.

Kellogg and colleagues measured separately contacted GaAs bilayers at total Landau filling one. Counterflow and parallel-current geometries show different Hall responses; the paper interprets the low-temperature counterflow trend as evidence for excitonic superfluidity. It also reports finite dissipation and no expected nonlinear signature in the examined range. These quantum-Hall conditions are not evidence for exciton-mediated charged Cooper pairing in an arbitrary van der Waals bilayer. 

Mitrano and colleagues' earlier K3C60 manuscript reports transient superconducting-like optical features while considering a high-mobility alternative within its finite probe window. The existing source check leaves a final-publication update unresolved. Budden and colleagues add calibrated electrical measurements: their author manuscript uses a 1 ns two-terminal probe and subtracts contact contributions inferred from static four-terminal measurements. At a 100 K base temperature, the reported transient resistance is compatible with zero within calibration uncertainty. This is not a direct transient four-terminal measurement, and 100 K is not entered as an equilibrium transition temperature.  

 Limits and disputes

Inkson and Anderson argued that double counting in a metal–semiconductor interaction treatment removes the proposed excitonic enhancement. Allender, Bray and Bardeen replied that the criticized model differs from theirs and stressed dielectric spectral weight over a broad momentum range. Both publisher abstracts are retained. This historical exchange identifies a screening and model-consistency problem; it does not by itself establish either a universal mechanism or a universal prohibition.  

Aranzadi and colleagues' 2026 preprint, version 2, proposes a purely electronic two-photon pathway for light-enhanced pair correlations. Its 14-site one-orbital calculation reaches roughly 30 THz, still above the experimental 10 THz reference scale. In one parameter range the calculation starts in the lowest even-parity state rather than the odd ground state; initialization matters. The paper explicitly leaves relevant decay channels outside its isolated dynamics. Finite-cluster correlations and a suggested scaling trend do not establish bulk phase coherence, a metastable lifetime or the classic virtual-exciton mechanism. The source remains a preprint. 

Ganin and colleagues' equilibrium Cs3C60 report is a separate fulleride evidence chain. Its 38 K publication title is retained as bibliographic information; this entry has not audited the complete pressure, sample and transition protocol and does not add a material record from the title. Neither that result nor photo-driven K3C60 independently identifies exciton-mediated pairing. 

 Discovery implications

Evaluate an interface proposal by its accessible electronic spectrum, wavefunction overlap and complete screened interaction, including normal-state effects. State whether an observed current is charged coflow, neutral counterflow or a pump-induced transient. Preserve contradictory measurements and preparation details. Mechanism discrimination requires predictions that survive competing explanations; a large model energy scale or a nonlinear optical response is insufficient. Full scientific, final-version and raw-data audits remain open.

entries.title: Plasmon-mediated pairing and dynamical screening
entries.summary: Understand collective charge modes, dielectric screening and pairing proposals without confusing a measured plasmon with proof of its superconducting role.

entries.text:
Scope

Plasmon-mediated pairing is a proposal in which the frequency-dependent screening of Coulomb interactions contributes to a superconducting pairing kernel. A plasmon is a collective charge oscillation; it is not an exciton, a static charge-density wave or an acoustic phonon. Observing a charge mode establishes something available to couple to electrons, not the cause of their superconductivity.

Takada's early electron-gas calculation used weak coupling and a plasmon-pole approximation to examine dimensionality. Akashi and Arita later developed a dynamical superconducting density-functional kernel and predicted cooperative phonon–plasmon enhancement for compressed fcc lithium. These are calculations under specified approximations, not experimental isolation of a universal pairing mechanism. Only their publisher abstracts have been checked here.  

 Mathematical assumptions

In a homogeneous scalar description, the screened interaction is W(q,z)=Vq/\epsilon(q,z). Crystals and interfaces can require dielectric matrices and wavefunction matrix elements. A longitudinal collective mode is associated with a pole of the response; with damping its frequency is complex. A zero of \operatorname{Re}\epsilon on the real axis is not a complete mode definition. The measured loss function -\operatorname{Im}\epsilon^{-1} also contains line-shape information.

An independent Drude illustration normalizes the background dielectric constant to one and assumes plasma frequency \omegap and damping rate \gamma:

\epsilon(z)=1-\frac{\omegap^2}{z(z+i\gamma)},\qquad z\pm=-\frac{i\gamma}{2}\pm\sqrt{\omegap^2-\frac{\gamma^2}{4}}.

Direct complex substitution and numerical loss maximization were checked for four damping ratios. At \gamma/\omegap=0.5, the positive real-part zero is approximately 0.866\omegap, the real part of the pole is 0.96825\omegap, and the loss maximum is 0.96877\omegap. They are different quantities. For stronger damping a loss maximum can remain even without a real-axis dielectric zero; it does not guarantee a long-lived excitation.

With damping set to zero and imaginary frequency i\nu, the same illustration gives

\frac{W(i\nu)}{V}=1-\frac{\omegap^2}{\nu^2+\omegap^2}=\frac{\nu^2}{\nu^2+\omegap^2}.

Five direct evaluations are nonnegative despite the negative retarded term in the decomposition. Removing the instantaneous term would change the model. This long-wavelength expression must not be substituted for finite-momentum static screening. Whether a frequency-dependent interaction supports pairing requires the full gap equation, normal self-energy and a defensible treatment of high-energy states; the sign of one separated term is insufficient.

Geometry also changes the modes. For two identical ideal electron sheets separated by d, with no tunneling and a hydrodynamic density response, diagonalizing the Coulomb layer matrix gives

\omega\pm^2=Cq\left(1\pm e^{-qd}\right),\qquad C=\frac{2\pi n{2D}e^2}{\kappa m}.

Here q is the in-plane wavevector magnitude, \kappa the background permittivity and Gaussian electrostatic units are used. In the qd\ll1 limit, the in-phase mode scales as \sqrt{2Cq} and the out-of-phase mode as q\sqrt{Cd}. Four direct matrix checks recover these limits. The illustration omits tunneling, finite thickness, carrier pressure and the particle–hole continuum. A linear branch in this ideal model neither guarantees weak Landau damping nor describes every layered crystal.

A separate lossless ionic-screening illustration uses \epsilon{\mathrm{tot}}/\epsilon\infty=(\omegaL^2-z^2)/(\omegaT^2-z^2)-\omegae^2/z^2, where \omegaL>\omegaT>0 describe one polar oscillator and \omegae is the electronic plasma scale screened only by \epsilon\infty. Its squared mode frequencies satisfy x^2-(\omegaL^2+\omegae^2)x+\omegae^2\omegaT^2=0. Direct root searches agree with the quadratic roots for five normalized examples. At low electronic plasma scale the lower branch approaches \omegae\omegaT/\omegaL; at high scale it approaches \omegaT. This demonstrates hybridization, not a calculated material transition temperature.

 Experimental criteria

Measure the charge response over the momentum and energy window relevant to the electrons, including linewidths, polarization, dielectric surroundings and calibration. Optical measurements near zero momentum and finite-momentum scattering constrain different parts of the problem. A pairing attribution additionally needs a screened interaction consistent with the band structure, normal response and superconducting observations on comparable samples.

Hepting and colleagues' 2018 electron-doped cuprate study used polarization and momentum dependence to identify collective charge excitations with out-of-plane dispersion. Its publisher abstract supports the mode assignment; this entry has not independently reanalyzed its spectra or extracted a pairing interaction from them. 

Their 2022 published SLCO study reports Cu-edge RIXS at 20 K with about 40 meV energy resolution and an approximately 120 meV plasmon gap. Near |H|\le0.005 reciprocal lattice units, overlap with a phonon prevents unambiguous peak fitting; these points were excluded from the model fit. The authors describe an acousticlike but gapped branch and interpret its dispersion using a layered model with interlayer hopping. The measurement temperature and mode gap are not superconducting transition temperatures or direct pairing evidence. 

 Limits and disputes

Ruhman and Lee's dilute SrTiO3 proposal requires dielectric screening weaker than in the insulating material to obtain its reported pairing scale. The accepted manuscript treats the dielectric response and a high-energy renormalization parameter phenomenologically and restricts the weak-coupling calculation's energy window. Agreement with a superconducting dome therefore does not independently measure the plasmon contribution. Selected accepted-manuscript passages were checked after comparison with the earlier arXiv version; complete model reproduction remains open. 

Davydov and colleagues compared dynamical Coulomb treatments in Eliashberg theory, superconducting density-functional theory and a hybrid approach. Their calculations demonstrate that Coulomb effects in the normal self-energy can oppose enhancement in the pairing channel, and that different approximations produce different transition estimates. The earlier manuscript's selected equations and the final publisher abstract were checked; full final-version comparison is still pending. The study is not a theorem excluding all plasmon mechanisms. 

One must not append an attractive plasmon term to a repulsion that already includes the same screening without checking for double counting. Nor does a high collective-mode energy justify applying a phonon adiabatic approximation unchanged. Electronic scales, coupling strength, vertex corrections and competing fluctuations need explicit treatment. No independent calculation in this article solves a superconducting instability or certifies a material mechanism.

 Discovery implications

For a dielectric or layered-material proposal, track how controlled density, spacing or screening changes affect both the collective response and superconducting observables. Separate changes in band filling, disorder, structural phase and phonons from the proposed charge-mode effect. Preserve negative results and uncertainty. The useful target is a testable quantitative mechanism with identifiable assumptions, not a ranking based on the largest observed plasmon energy. Full scientific acceptance remains open.
